arXiv:2310.02541v1 [cs.LG] 04 Oct 2023

Benign Overfitting and Grokking
in ReLU Networks for XOR Cluster Data

Zhiwei Xu Affiliation: University of Michigan Email: zhiweixu@umich.edu    Yutong Wang Affiliation: University of Michigan Email: yutongw@umich.edu    Spencer Frei Affiliation: University of California, Davis Email: sfrei@ucdavis.edu    Gal Vardi Affiliation: TTI-Chicago and Hebrew University Email: galvardi@ttic.edu    Wei Hu Affiliation: University of Michigan Email: vvh@umich.edu
Abstract

Neural networks trained by gradient descent (GD) have exhibited a number of surprising generalization behaviors. First, they can achieve a perfect fit to noisy training data and still generalize near-optimally, showing that overfitting can sometimes be benign. Second, they can undergo a period of classical, harmful overfitting—achieving a perfect fit to training data with near-random performance on test data—before transitioning (“grokking”) to near-optimal generalization later in training. In this work, we show that both of these phenomena provably occur in two-layer ReLU networks trained by GD on XOR cluster data where a constant fraction of the training labels are flipped. In this setting, we show that after the first step of GD, the network achieves 100% training accuracy, perfectly fitting the noisy labels in the training data, but achieves near-random test accuracy. At a later training step, the network achieves near-optimal test accuracy while still fitting the random labels in the training data, exhibiting a “grokking” phenomenon. This provides the first theoretical result of benign overfitting in neural network classification when the data distribution is not linearly separable. Our proofs rely on analyzing the feature learning process under GD, which reveals that the network implements a non-generalizable linear classifier after one step and gradually learns generalizable features in later steps.

1 Introduction

Classical wisdom in machine learning regards overfitting to noisy training data as harmful for generalization, and regularization techniques such as early stopping have been developed to prevent overfitting. However, modern neural networks can exhibit a number of counterintuitive phenomena that contravene this classical wisdom. Two intriguing phenomena that have attracted significant attention in recent years are benign overfitting [Bar+20] and grokking [Pow+22]:

  • •

    Benign overfitting: A model perfectly fits noisily labeled training data, but still achieves near-optimal test error.

  • •

    Grokking: A model initially achieves perfect training accuracy but no generalization (i.e. no better than a random predictor), and upon further training, transitions to almost perfect generalization.

Recent theoretical work has established benign overfitting in a variety of settings, including linear regression [Has+19, Bar+20], linear classification [CL21a, WT21], kernel methods [BRT19, LR20], and neural network classification [FCB22a, Kou+23]. However, existing results of benign overfitting in neural network classification settings are restricted to linearly separable data distributions, leaving open the question of how benign overfitting can occur in fully non-linear settings. For grokking, several recent papers [Nan+23, Gro23, Var+23] have proposed explanations, but to the best of our knowledge, no prior work has established a rigorous proof of grokking in a neural network setting.

In this work, we characterize a setting in which both benign overfitting and grokking provably occur. We consider a two-layer ReLU network trained by gradient descent on a binary classification task defined by an XOR cluster data distribution (Figure 2). Specifically, datapoints from the positive class are drawn from a mixture of two high-dimensional Gaussian distributions 12​N​(μ1,I)+12​N​(−μ1,I)\frac{1}{2}N(\mu_{1},I)+\frac{1}{2}N(-\mu_{1},I), and datapoints from the negative class are drawn from 12​N​(μ2,I)+12​N​(−μ2,I)\frac{1}{2}N(\mu_{2},I)+\frac{1}{2}N(-\mu_{2},I), where μ1\mu_{1} and μ2\mu_{2} are orthogonal vectors. We then allow a constant fraction of the labels to be flipped. In this setting, we rigorously prove the following results: (i) One-step catastrophic overfitting: After one gradient descent step, the network perfectly fits every single training datapoint (no matter if it has a clean or flipped label), but has test accuracy close to 50%50\%, performing no better than random guessing. (ii) Grokking and benign overfitting: After training for more steps, the network undergoes a “grokking” period from catastrophic to benign overfitting—it eventually reaches near 100%100\% test accuracy, while maintaining 100%100\% training accuracy the whole time. This behavior can be seen in Figure 1, where we also see that with a smaller step size the same grokking phenomenon occurs but with a delayed time for both overfitting and generalization.

Our results provide the first theoretical characterization of benign overfitting in a truly non-linear setting involving training a neural network on a non-linearly separable distribution. Interestingly, prior work on benign overfitting in neural networks for linearly separable distributions [FCB22a, Cao+22, XG23, Kou+23] have not shown a time separation between catastrophic overfitting and generalization, which suggests that the XOR cluster data setting is fundamentally different.

Our proofs rely on analyzing the feature learning behavior of individual neurons over the gradient descent trajectory. After one training step, we prove that the network approximately implements a linear classifier over the underlying data distribution, which is able to overfit all the training datapoints but unable to generalize. Upon further training, the neurons gradually align with the core features ±μ1\pm\mu_{1} and ±μ2\pm\mu_{2}, which is sufficient for generalization. See Figure 2 for visualizations of the network’s decision boundary and neuron weights at different time steps, which confirm our theory.

1.1 Additonal Related Work

Benign overfitting.

The literature on benign overfitting (also known as harmless interpolation) is now immense; for a general overview, we refer the readers to the surveys [BMR21, Bel21, DMB21]. We focus here on those works on benign overfitting in neural networks. [FCB22a] showed that two-layer networks with smooth leaky ReLU activations trained by gradient descent (GD) exhibit benign overfitting when trained on a high-dimensional binary cluster distribution. [XG23] extended their results to more general activations like ReLU. [Cao+22] showed that two-layer convolutional networks with polynomial-ReLU activations trained by GD exhibit benign overfitting for image-patch data; [Kou+23] extended their results to allow for label-flipping noise and standard ReLU activations. Each of these works used a trajectory-based analysis and none of them identified a grokking phenomenon. [Fre+23, KYS23] showed how stationary points of margin-maximization problems associated with homogeneous neural network training problems can exhibit benign overfitting. Finally, [Mal+22] proposed a taxonomy of overfitting behaviors in neural networks, whereby overfitting is “catastrophic” if test-time performance is comparable to a random guess, “benign” if it is near-optimal, and “tempered” if it lies between catastrophic and benign.

Grokking.

The phenomenon of grokking was first identified by [Pow+22] in decoder-only transformers trained on algorithmic datasets. [Liu+22] provided an effective theory of representation learning to understand grokking. [Thi+22] attributed grokking to the slingshot mechanism, which can be measured by the cyclic phase transitions between stable and unstable training regimes. [ŽI22] showed a time separation between achieving zero training error and zero test error in a binary classification task on a linearly separable distribution. [LMT23] identified a large initialization scale together with weight decay as a mechanism for grokking. [Bar+22, Nan+23] proposed progress metrics to measure the progress towards generalization during training. [DLK23] hypothesized a pattern-learning model for grokking and first reported a model-wise grokking phenomenon. [MTS23] studied the learning dynamics in a two-layer neural network on a sparse parity task, attributing grokking to the competition between dense and sparse subnetworks. [Var+23] utilized circuit efficiency to interpret grokking and discovered two novel phenomena called ungrokking and semi-grokking.

Feature learning for XOR distributions.

The behavior of neural networks trained on the XOR cluster distribution we consider here, or its variants like the sparse parity problem, have been extensively studied in recent years. [Wei+19] showed that neural networks in the mean-field regime, where neural networks can learn features, have better sample complexity guarantees than neural networks in the neural tangent kernel (NTK) regime in this setting. [Bar+22, Tel23] examined the sample complexity of learning sparse parities on the hypercube for neural networks trained by SGD. Most related to this work, [FCB22] characterized the dynamics of GD in ReLU networks in the same distributional setting we consider here, namely the XOR cluster with label-flipping noise. They showed that by early-stopping, the neural network achieves perfect (clean) test accuracy although the training error is close to the label noise rate; in particular, their network achieved optimal generalization without overfitting, which is fundamentally different from our result. By contrast, we show that the network first exhibits catastrophic overfitting before transitioning to benign overfitting later in training.11 1 The reason for the different behaviors between our work and [FCB22] is because they work in a setting with a larger signal-to-noise ratio (i.e., the norm of the cluster means is larger than the one we consider).

2.2 Data Generation Setting

Let μ1,μ2∈ℝp\mu_{1},\mu_{2}\in\mathbb{R}^{p} be two orthogonal vectors, i.e. μ1⊤​μ2=0\mu_{1}^{\top}\mu_{2}=0.22 2 Our results hold when μ1\mu_{1} and μ2\mu_{2} are near-orthogonal. We assume exact orthogonality for ease of presentation. Let η∈[0,1/2)\eta\in[0,1/2) be the label flipping probability.

Definition 2.1 (XOR cluster data).

Define PcleanP_{\text{clean}} as the distribution over the space ℝp×{±1}{\mathbb{R}}^{p}\times\{\pm 1\} of labelled data such that a datapoint (x,y~)∼Pclean(x,\widetilde{y})\sim P_{\text{clean}} is generated according to the following procedure: First, sample the label y~∼Unif​{±1}\widetilde{y}\sim\text{Unif}\{\pm 1\}. Second, generate xx as follows:

  1. (1)

    If y~=1\widetilde{y}=1, then x∼12​N​(+μ1,Ip)+12​N​(−μ1,Ip)x\sim\frac{1}{2}N(+\mu_{1},I_{p})+\frac{1}{2}N(-\mu_{1},I_{p});

  2. (2)

    If y~=−1\widetilde{y}=-1, then x∼12​N​(+μ2,Ip)+12​N​(−μ2,Ip)x\sim\frac{1}{2}N(+\mu_{2},I_{p})+\frac{1}{2}N(-\mu_{2},I_{p}).

Define PP to be the distribution over ℝp×{±1}{\mathbb{R}}^{p}\times\{\pm 1\} which is the η\eta-noise-corrupted version of PcleanP_{\text{clean}}, namely: to generate a sample (x,y)∼P(x,y)\sim P, first generate (x,y~)∼Pclean(x,\widetilde{y})\sim P_{\text{clean}}, and then let y=y~y=\widetilde{y} with probability 1−η1-\eta, and y=−y~y=-\widetilde{y} with probability η\eta.

We consider nn training datapoints {(xi,yi)}i=1n\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} generated i.i.d from the distribution PP. We assume the sample size nn to be sufficiently large (i.e., larger than any universal constant appearing in this paper). Note the xix_{i}’s are from a mixture of four Gaussians centered at ±μ1\pm\mu_{1} and ±μ2\pm\mu_{2}. We denote 𝖼𝖾𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗌:={±μ1,±μ2}\mathsf{centers}:=\{\pm\mu_{1},\pm\mu_{2}\} for convenience. For simplicity, we assume ‖μ1‖=‖μ2‖\|\mu_{1}\|=\|\mu_{2}\|, omit the subscripts and denote them by ‖μ‖\|\mu\|.

3 Main Results

Given a large enough universal constant CC, we make the following assumptions:

  1. (A1)

    The norm of the mean satisfies ‖μ‖2≥C​n0.51​p\|\mu\|^{2}\geq Cn^{0.51}\sqrt{p}.

  2. (A2)

    The dimension of the feature space satisfies p≥C​n2​‖μ‖2p\geq Cn^{2}\|\mu\|^{2}.

  3. (A3)

    The noise rate satisfies η≤1/C\eta\leq 1/C.

  4. (A4)

    The step size satisfies α≤1/(C​n​p).\alpha\leq 1/(Cnp).

  5. (A5)

    The initialization variance satisfies ωinit ​n​m3/2​p≤α​‖μ‖2\omega_{\text{init }}nm^{3/2}p\leq\alpha\|\mu\|^{2}.

  6. (A6)

    The number of neurons satisfies m≥C​n0.02m\geq Cn^{0.02}.

Assumption (A1) concerns the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in the distribution, where the order 0.510.51 can be extended to any constant strictly larger than 12\tfrac{1}{2}. The assumption of high-dimensionality (A2) is important for enabling benign overfitting, and implies that the training datapoints are near-orthogonal. For a given nn, these two assumptions are simultaneously satisfied if ‖μ‖=Θ⁡(pβ)\|\mu\|=\Theta(p^{\beta}) where β∈(14,12)\beta\in(\tfrac{1}{4},\tfrac{1}{2}) and pp is a sufficiently large polynomial in nn. Assumption (A3) ensures that the label noise rate is at most a constant. While Assumption (A4) ensures the step size is small enough to allow for a variant of smoothness between different steps, Assumption (A5) ensures that the step size is large relative to the initialization scale so that the behavior of the network after a single step of GD is significantly different from that at random initialization. Assumption (A6) ensures the number of neurons is large enough to allow for concentration arguments at random initialization.

With these assumptions in place, we can state our main theorem which characterizes the training error and test error of the neural network at different times during the training trajectory.

Theorem 3.1.

Suppose that Assumptions (A1)-(A6) hold. With probability at least 1−n−Ω⁡(1)−O⁡(1/m)1-n^{-\Omega(1)}-O(1/\sqrt{m}) over the random data generation and initialization of the weights, we have:

  • •

    The classifier sgn⁡(f⁡(x,W(t)))\operatorname{sgn}(f(x;W^{(t)})) can correctly classify all training datapoints for 1≤t≤n1\leq t\leq\sqrt{n}:

    yi=sgn⁡(f⁡(xi,W(t))),∀i∈[n].y_{i}=\operatorname{sgn}(f(x_{i};W^{(t)})),\quad\forall i\in[n].
  • •

    The classifier sgn⁡(f⁡(x,W(t)))\operatorname{sgn}(f(x;W^{(t)})) has near-random test error at t=1t=1:

    12​(1−n−Ω⁡(1))≤ℙ(x,y)∼Pclean​(y≠sgn⁡(f⁡(x,W(1))))≤12​(1+n−Ω⁡(1)).\tfrac{1}{2}(1-n^{-\Omega(1)})\leq{\mathbb{P}}_{(x,y)\sim P_{\text{clean}}}(y\neq\operatorname{sgn}(f(x;W^{(1)})))\leq\tfrac{1}{2}(1+n^{-\Omega(1)}).
  • •

    The classifier sgn⁡(f⁡(x,W(t)))\operatorname{sgn}(f(x;W^{(t)})) generalizes when C​n0.01≤t≤nCn^{0.01}\leq t\leq\sqrt{n}:

    ℙ(x,y)∼Pclean​(y≠sgn⁡(f⁡(x,W(t))))≤exp⁡(−Ω⁡(n0.99​‖μ‖4/p))=exp⁡(−Ω⁡(n2.01)).\mathbb{P}_{(x,y)\sim P_{\text{clean}}}(y\neq\operatorname{sgn}(f(x;W^{(t)})))\leq\exp(-\Omega(n^{0.99}\|\mu\|^{4}/p))=\exp(-\Omega(n^{2.01})).

Theorem 3.1 shows that at time t=1t=1, the network achieves 100% training accuracy despite the constant fraction of flipped labels in the training data. The second part of the theorem shows that this overfitting is catastrophic as the test error is close to that of a random guess. On the other hand, by the first and third parts of the theorem, as long as the time step tt satisfies C​n0.01≤t≤nCn^{0.01}\leq t\leq\sqrt{n}, the network continues to overfit to the training data while simultaneously achieving test error exp⁡(−Ω⁡(n2.01))\exp(-\Omega(n^{2.01})), which guarantees a near-zero test error for large nn. In particular, the network exhibits benign overfitting, and it achieves this by grokking. Notably, Theorem 3.1 is the first guarantee for benign overfitting in neural network classification for a nonlinear data distribution, in contrast to prior works which required linearly separable distributions [FCB22a, Fre+23, Cao+22, XG23, Kou+23, KYS23].

We note that Theorem 3.1 requires an upper bound on the number of iterations of gradient descent, i.e. it does not provide a guarantee as t→∞t\to\infty. At a technical level, this is needed so that we can guarantee that the ratio of the sigmoid losses between all samples r⁡(t):=maxi,j∈[n]⁡gi(t)gj(t)r(t):=\max_{i,j\in[n]}\tfrac{g_{i}^{(t)}}{g_{j}^{(t)}} is close to 11, and we show that this holds if t≤nt\leq\sqrt{n}. This property prevents the training data with flipped labels from having an out-sized influence on the feature learning dynamics. Prior works in other settings have shown that r⁡(t)r(t) is at most a large constant for any step tt for a similar purpose [FCB22a, XG23], however the dynamics of learning in the XOR setting are more intricate and require a tighter bound on r⁡(t)r(t). We leave the question of generalizing our results to longer training times for future work.

In Section 4, we provide an overview of the key ingredients to the proof of Theorem 3.1.

In Section 4.1, we present several properties satisfied with high probability by the training data and random initialization, which are crucial in our proof. In Section 4.2, we outline the major steps in the proof of Theorem 3.1.

4.1 Properties of the Training Data and Random Initialization

Lemma 4.1 (Properties of training data).

Suppose Assumptions (A1) and (A2) hold. Let the training data {(xi,yi)}i=1n\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n} be sampled i.i.d from PP as in Definition 2.1. With probability at least 1−O⁡(n−ε)1-O(n^{-\varepsilon}) the training data satisfy properties (B1)-(B4) defined below.

  1. (B1)

  2. (B2)

    For each i,k∈[n]i,k\in[n] such that i≠ki\neq k, we have |⟨xi,xk⟩−⟨x¯i,x¯k⟩|≤10​p​log⁡n.|\langle x_{i},x_{k}\rangle-\langle\bar{x}_{i},\bar{x}_{k}\rangle|\leq 10\sqrt{p\log n}.

  3. (B3)

    For ν∈𝖼𝖾𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗌\nu\in\mathsf{centers}, we have |cν+nν−n/4|≤ε​n​log⁡n|c_{\nu}+n_{\nu}-n/4|\leq\sqrt{\varepsilon n\log n} and |nν−η⁡(cν+nν)|≤ε​η​n​log⁡n|n_{\nu}-\eta(c_{\nu}+n_{\nu})|\leq\sqrt{\varepsilon\eta n\log n}.

  4. (B4)

    For ν∈𝖼𝖾𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗌\nu\in\mathsf{centers}, we have |cν+nν−c−ν−n−ν|≥n1/2−ε|c_{\nu}+n_{\nu}-c_{-\nu}-n_{-\nu}|\geq n^{1/2-\varepsilon} and |nν−n−ν|≥η​n1/2−ε|n_{\nu}-n_{-\nu}|\geq\eta n^{1/2-\varepsilon}.

Denote by 𝒢data\mathcal{G}_{\text{data}} the set of training data satisfying conditions (B1)-(B4). Thus, the result can be stated succinctly as ℙ⁡(X∈𝒢data)≥1−O⁡(n−ε){\mathbb{P}}(X\in\mathcal{G}_{\text{data}})\geq 1-O(n^{-\varepsilon}).

The proof of Lemma 4.1 can be found in Section A.2.1. Conditions (B1) and (B2) are essentially the same as [FCB22a, Lemma 4.3] or [CL21, Lemma 10]. Conditions (B3) and (B4) concern the number of clean and noisy examples in each cluster, and can be proved by concentration and anti-concentration arguments, respectively.

Lemma 4.1 has an important corollary.

Corollary 4.2 (Near-orthogonality of training data).

Suppose Assumptions (A1), (A2), and Conditions (B1), (B2) from Lemma 4.1 all hold. Then

|cossim⁡(xi,xk)|≤2C​n2|\mathrm{cossim}(x_{i},x_{k})|\leq\frac{2}{Cn^{2}}

for all 1≤i≠k≤n1\leq i\neq k\leq n.

This near-orthogonality comes from the high dimensionality of the feature space (i.e., Assumption (A2)) and will be crucially used throughout the proofs on optimization and generalization of the network. The proof of Corollary 4.2 can be found in Section A.2.1.

Next, we divide the neuron indices into two sets according to the sign of the corresponding second-layer weight:

𝒥𝙿𝚘𝚜:={j∈[m]:aj>0};𝒥𝙽𝚎𝚐:={j∈[m]:aj<0}.\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Pos}}}:=\{j\in[m]:a_{j}>0\};\quad\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Neg}}}:=\{j\in[m]:a_{j}<0\}.

We will conveniently call them positive and negative neurons. Our next lemma shows that some properties of the random initialization hold with a large probability. The proof details can be found in Section A.3.1.

Lemma 4.3 (Properties of the random weight initialization).

Suppose Assumptions (A1), (A2) and (A6) hold. The followings hold with probability at least 1−O⁡(n−ε)1-O(n^{-\varepsilon}) over the random initialization:

  1. (C1)

    ‖W(0)‖F2≤32​ωinit 2​m​p.\big\|W^{(0)}\big\|_{F}^{2}\leq\frac{3}{2}\omega_{\text{init }}^{2}mp.

  2. (C2)

    |𝒥𝙿𝚘𝚜|≥m/3|\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Pos}}}|\geq m/3 and |𝒥𝙽𝚎𝚐|≥m/3|\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Neg}}}|\geq m/3.

Denote the set of W(0)W^{(0)} satisfying condition (C1) by 𝒢W\mathcal{G}_{W}. Denote the set of a=(aj)j=1ma=(a_{j})_{j=1}^{m} satisfying condition (C2) by 𝒢A\mathcal{G}_{A}. Then ℙ⁡(a∈𝒢A,W(0)∈𝒢W)≥1−O⁡(n−ε){\mathbb{P}}(a\in\mathcal{G}_{A},W^{(0)}\in\mathcal{G}_{W})\geq 1-O(n^{-\varepsilon}).

We say that the sample ii activates neuron jj at time tt if ⟨wj(t),xi⟩>0\langle w_{j}^{(t)},x_{i}\rangle>0. Now, for each neuron j∈[m]j\in[m], time t≥0t\geq 0 and ν∈𝖼𝖾𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗌\nu\in\mathsf{centers}, define the set of indices ii of samples xix_{i} with clean (resp. noisy) labels from the cluster centered at ν\nu that activates neuron jj at time tt:

𝒞ν,j(t):={i∈𝒞ν:⟨wj(t),xi⟩>0}(resp. ​𝒩ν,j(t):={i∈𝒩ν:⟨wj(t),xi⟩>0}​).\mathcal{C}_{\nu,j}^{(t)}:=\{i\in{\mathcal{C}}_{\nu}:\langle w_{j}^{(t)},x_{i}\rangle>0\}\quad\mbox{(resp. }\mathcal{N}_{\nu,j}^{(t)}:=\{i\in{\mathcal{N}}_{\nu}:\langle w_{j}^{(t)},x_{i}\rangle>0\}\mbox{)}. (4.1)

Moreover, we define

dν,j(t):=|𝒞ν,j(t)|−|𝒩ν,j(t)|,andDν,j(t):=dν,j(t)−d−ν,j(t).d_{\nu,j}^{(t)}:=|\mathcal{C}_{\nu,j}^{(t)}|-|\mathcal{N}_{\nu,j}^{(t)}|,\quad\mbox{and}\quad D_{\nu,j}^{(t)}:=d_{\nu,j}^{(t)}-d_{-\nu,j}^{(t)}.

For κ∈[0,1/2)\kappa\in[0,1/2) and ν∈𝖼𝖾𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗌\nu\in\mathsf{centers}, a neuron jj is said to be (ν,κ)(\nu,\kappa)-aligned if

Dν,j(0)>n1/2−κ,andmax⁡{d−ν,j(0),dν,j(0)}<min⁡{cν,c−ν}−2​(n+ν+n−ν)−nD_{\nu,j}^{(0)}>n^{1/2-\kappa},\quad\mbox{and}\quad\max\{d_{-\nu,j}^{(0)},d_{\nu,j}^{(0)}\}<\min\{c_{\nu},c_{-\nu}\}-2(n_{+\nu}+n_{-\nu})-\sqrt{n} (4.2)

The first condition ensures that at initialization, there are at least n1/2−κn^{1/2-\kappa} many more samples from cluster ν\nu activating the jj-th neuron than from cluster −ν-\nu after accounting for cancellations from the noisy labels. The second is a technical condition necessary for trajectory analysis. A neuron jj is said to be (±ν,κ)(\pm\nu,\kappa)-aligned if it is either (ν,κ)(\nu,\kappa)-aligned or (−ν,κ)(-\nu,\kappa)-aligned.

Lemma 4.4 (Properties of the interaction between training data and initial weights).

Suppose Assumptions (A1)-(A3) and (A6) hold. Given a∈𝒢A,X∈𝒢dataa\in\mathcal{G}_{A},X\in\mathcal{G}_{\text{data}}, the followings hold with probability at least 1−O⁡(n−ε)1-O(n^{-\varepsilon}) over the random initialization W(0)W^{(0)}:

  1. (D1)

    For all i∈[n]i\in[n], the sample xix_{i} activates a large proportion of positive and negative neurons, i.e., |{j∈𝒥𝙿𝚘𝚜:⟨wj(0),xi⟩>0}|≥m/7|\{j\in\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Pos}}}:\langle w_{j}^{(0)},x_{i}\rangle>0\}|\geq m/7 and |{j∈𝒥𝙽𝚎𝚐:⟨wj(0),xi⟩>0}|≥m/7|\{j\in\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Neg}}}:\langle w_{j}^{(0)},x_{i}\rangle>0\}|\geq m/7 both hold.

  2. (D2)

    For all ν∈𝖼𝖾𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗌\nu\in\mathsf{centers} and κ∈[0,12)\kappa\in[0,\tfrac{1}{2}), both |{j∈𝒥𝙿𝚘𝚜:j is (ν,κ)-aligned}|≥m​n−10​ε|\{j\in\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Pos}}}:\mbox{$j$ is $(\nu,\kappa)$-aligned}\}|\geq mn^{-10\varepsilon}, and |{j∈𝒥𝙽𝚎𝚐:j is (ν,κ)-aligned}|≥m​n−10​ε|\{j\in\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Neg}}}:\mbox{$j$ is $(\nu,\kappa)$-aligned}\}|\geq mn^{-10\varepsilon}.

  3. (D3)

    For all ν∈𝖼𝖾𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗌\nu\in\mathsf{centers}, we have |{j∈𝒥𝙿𝚘𝚜:j is (±ν,20​ε)-aligned}|≥(1−10​n−20​ε)​|𝒥𝙿𝚘𝚜|\big|\{j\in\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Pos}}}:\mbox{$j$ is $(\pm\nu,20\varepsilon)$-aligned}\}\big|\geq(1-10n^{-20\varepsilon})|\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Pos}}}|. Moreover, the same statement holds if “𝒥𝙿𝚘𝚜\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Pos}}}” is replaced with “𝒥𝙽𝚎𝚐\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Neg}}}” everywhere.

  4. (D4)

    For all ν∈𝖼𝖾𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗌\nu\in\mathsf{centers} and κ∈[0,12)\kappa\in[0,\tfrac{1}{2}), let 𝒥ν,𝙿𝚘𝚜κ:={j∈𝒥𝙿𝚘𝚜:j is (ν,κ)-aligned}\mathcal{J}_{\nu,{\mathtt{Pos}}}^{\kappa}:=\{j\in\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Pos}}}:\mbox{$j$ is $(\nu,\kappa)$-aligned}\}. Then ∑j∈𝒥ν,𝙿𝚘𝚜κ(cν−nν−d−ν,j(0))≥n10​|𝒥ν,𝙿𝚘𝚜κ|\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{\nu,{\mathtt{Pos}}}^{\kappa}}(c_{\nu}-n_{\nu}-d_{-\nu,j}^{(0)})\geq\frac{n}{10}|\mathcal{J}_{\nu,{\mathtt{Pos}}}^{\kappa}|. Moreover, the same statement holds if “𝒥𝙿𝚘𝚜\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Pos}}}” is replaced with “𝒥𝙽𝚎𝚐\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Neg}}}” everywhere.

Condition (D1) makes sure that the neurons spread uniformly at initialization so that each datapoint activates at least a constant fraction of positive and negative neurons. Condition (D2) guarantees that for each ν∈𝖼𝖾𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗌\nu\in\mathsf{centers}, there are a fraction of neurons aligning with ν\nu more than −ν-\nu. Condition (D3) shows that most neurons will somewhat align with either ν\nu or −ν-\nu. Condition (D4) is a technical concentration result. For proof details, see Section A.3.2.

Define the set 𝒢good\mathcal{G}_{\text{good}} as

𝒢good:={(a,W(0),X):a∈𝒢A,X∈𝒢data,W(0)∈𝒢W and conditions (D1)-(D4) hold},\mathcal{G}_{\text{good}}:=\{(a,W^{(0)},X):a\in\mathcal{G}_{A},X\in\mathcal{G}_{\text{data}},W^{(0)}\in\mathcal{G}_{W}\text{ and conditions \ref{B_main_1}-\ref{B_main_4} hold}\},

whose probability is lower bounded by ℙ⁡((a,W(0),X)∈𝒢good)≥1−O⁡(n−ε){\mathbb{P}}((a,W^{(0)},X)\in\mathcal{G}_{\text{good}})\geq 1-O(n^{-\varepsilon}). This is a consequence of Lemmas 4.1, 4.3 and 4.4 (see Section A.3.3).

Definition 4.5.

If the training data XX and the initialization a,W(0)a,W^{(0)} belong to 𝒢good\mathcal{G}_{\text{good}}, we define this circumstance as a “good run.”

4.2 Proof Sketch for Theorem 3.1

In order for the network to learn a generalizable solution for the XOR cluster distribution, we would like positive neurons’ (i.e., those with aj>0a_{j}>0) weights wjw_{j} to align with ±μ1\pm\mu_{1}, and negative neurons’ weights to align with ±μ2\pm\mu_{2}; we prove that this is satisfied for t∈[C​n0.01,n]t\in[Cn^{0.01},\sqrt{n}]. However, for t=1t=1, we show that the network only approximates a linear classifier, which can fit the training data in high dimension but has trivial test error. Figure 3 plots the evolution of the distribution of positive neurons’ projections onto both μ1\mu_{1} and μ2\mu_{2}, confirming that these neurons are much more aligned with ±μ1\pm\mu_{1} at a later training time, while they cannot distinguish ±μ1\pm\mu_{1} and ±μ2\pm\mu_{2} at t=1t=1.

Below we give a sketch of the proofs, and details are in Section A.5.

4.2.1 One-Step Catastrophic Overfitting

Under a good run, we have the following approximation for each neuron after the first iteration:

wj(1)≈α​aj2​n​∑i=1n𝕀⁡(⟨wj(0),xi⟩>0)​yi​xi,j∈[m].w_{j}^{(1)}\approx\frac{\alpha a_{j}}{2n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{I}(\langle w_{j}^{(0)},x_{i}\rangle>0)y_{i}x_{i},\quad j\in[m].

For details of this approximation, see Section A.4.

Let si​j:=𝕀⁡(⟨wj(0),xi⟩>0)s_{ij}:=\mathbb{I}(\langle w_{j}^{(0)},x_{i}\rangle>0). Then, for sufficiently large mm, we can approximate the neural network output at t=1t=1 as

∑j=1maj​ϕ​(⟨wj(1),x⟩)≈α2​n​∑j=1maj​ϕ​(aj​⟨∑i=1nsi​j​yi​xi,x⟩)→a.s.α4​n​⟨∑i=1n𝔼⁡[si​j]​yi​xi,x⟩=α8​n​⟨∑i=1nyi​xi,x⟩.\begin{split}\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_{j}\phi(\langle w_{j}^{(1)},x\rangle)&\approx\frac{\alpha}{2n}\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_{j}\phi(a_{j}\langle\sum_{i=1}^{n}s_{ij}y_{i}x_{i},x\rangle)\\ &\stackrel{{\scriptstyle a.s.}}{{\rightarrow}}\frac{\alpha}{4n}\langle\sum_{i=1}^{n}{\mathbb{E}}[s_{ij}]y_{i}x_{i},x\rangle=\frac{\alpha}{8n}\langle\sum_{i=1}^{n}y_{i}x_{i},x\rangle.\end{split} (4.3)

The convergence above follows from Lemma 4.6 below and that the first-layer weights and second-layer weights are independent at initialization. This implies that the neural network classifier sgn⁡(f⁡(⋅,W(1)))\operatorname{sgn}(f(\cdot;W^{(1)})) behaves similarly to the linear classifier sgn⁡(⟨∑i=1nyi​xi,⋅⟩)\operatorname{sgn}(\langle\sum_{i=1}^{n}y_{i}x_{i},\cdot\rangle). It can be shown that this linear classifier achieves 100% training accuracy whenever the training data are near orthogonal [Fre+23a, Appendix D], but because each class has two clusters with opposing means, linear classifiers only achieve 50% test error for the XOR cluster distribution. Thus at time t=1t=1, the network is able to fit the training data but is not capable of generalizing.

Lemma 4.6.

Let {aj}\{a_{j}\} and {bj}\{b_{j}\} be two independent sequences of random variables with aj∼i.i.d.Unif ​{±1m}a_{j}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle i.i.d.}}{{\sim}}\text{Unif }\{\pm\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\}, and 𝔼⁡[bj]=b,𝔼⁡[|bj|]<∞{\mathbb{E}}[b_{j}]=b,{\mathbb{E}}[|b_{j}|]<\infty. Then ∑j=1maj​ϕ​(aj​bj)→b/2\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_{j}\phi(a_{j}b_{j})\rightarrow b/2 almost surely as m→∞m\rightarrow\infty.

Proof.

Note that the ReLU function satisfies x=ϕ⁡(x)−ϕ⁡(−x)x=\phi(x)-\phi(-x), and 𝔼⁡[aj​ϕ​(aj​bj)]=𝔼⁡[ϕ⁡(bj)−ϕ⁡(−bj)]/2​m=𝔼⁡[bj]/2​m{\mathbb{E}}[a_{j}\phi(a_{j}b_{j})]={\mathbb{E}}[\phi(b_{j})-\phi(-b_{j})]/2m={\mathbb{E}}[b_{j}]/2m. Then the result follows from the strong law of large number. ∎

4.2.2 Multi-Step Generalization

Next, we show that positive (resp. negative) neurons gradually align with one of ±μ1\pm\mu_{1} (resp. ±μ2\pm\mu_{2}), and forget both of ±μ2\pm\mu_{2} (resp. ±μ1\pm\mu_{1}), making the network generalizable. Taking the direction +μ1+\mu_{1} as an example, we define sets of neurons

𝒥1={j∈𝒥𝙿𝚘𝚜:j is (+μ1,20​ε)-aligned};𝒥2={j∈𝒥𝙽𝚎𝚐:j is (±μ1,20​ε)-aligned}.\mathcal{J}_{1}=\{j\in\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Pos}}}:\mbox{$j$ is $(+\mu_{1},20\varepsilon)$-aligned}\};\quad\mathcal{J}_{2}=\{j\in\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Neg}}}:\mbox{$j$ is $(\pm\mu_{1},20\varepsilon)$-aligned}\}.

We have by conditions (D2)-(D3) of Lemma 4.4 that under a good run,

|𝒥1|≥m​n−10​ε,|𝒥2|≥(1−10​n−20​ε)​|𝒥𝙽𝚎𝚐|,|\mathcal{J}_{1}|\geq mn^{-10\varepsilon},\quad|\mathcal{J}_{2}|\geq(1-10n^{-20\varepsilon})|\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Neg}}}|,

which implies that 𝒥1\mathcal{J}_{1} contains a certain proportion of 𝒥𝙿𝚘𝚜\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Pos}}} and 𝒥2\mathcal{J}_{2} covers most of 𝒥𝙽𝚎𝚐\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Neg}}}. The next lemma shows that neurons in 𝒥1\mathcal{J}_{1} will keep aligning with +μ1+\mu_{1}, but neurons in 𝒥2\mathcal{J}_{2} will gradually forget +μ1+\mu_{1}.

Lemma 4.7.

Suppose that Assumptions (A1)-(A6) hold. Under a good run, we have that for 1≤t≤n1\leq t\leq\sqrt{n},

1|𝒥1|​∑j∈𝒥1⟨wj(t),+μ1⟩=Ω⁡(α​‖μ‖2m​t);\frac{1}{|\mathcal{J}_{1}|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{1}}\langle w_{j}^{(t)},+\mu_{1}\rangle=\Omega\left(\frac{\alpha\|\mu\|^{2}}{\sqrt{m}}t\right);
1|𝒥2|​∑j∈𝒥2|⟨wj(t),μ1⟩|=O⁡(α​‖μ‖2m+α​‖μ‖2​log⁡(n)m​n​t).\frac{1}{|\mathcal{J}_{2}|}\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{2}}|\langle w_{j}^{(t)},\mu_{1}\rangle|=O\left(\frac{\alpha\|\mu\|^{2}}{\sqrt{m}}+\frac{\alpha\|\mu\|^{2}\sqrt{\log(n)}}{\sqrt{mn}}t\right).

We can see that when tt is large, ∑j∈𝒥2|⟨wj(t),μ1⟩|/|𝒥2|=o⁡(∑j∈𝒥1⟨wj(t),+μ1⟩/|𝒥1|)\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{2}}|\langle w_{j}^{(t)},\mu_{1}\rangle|/|\mathcal{J}_{2}|=o(\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{1}}\langle w_{j}^{(t)},+\mu_{1}\rangle/|\mathcal{J}_{1}|), thus for x∼N⁡(+μ1,Ip)x\sim N(+\mu_{1},I_{p}), neurons with j∈𝒥1j\in\mathcal{J}_{1} will dominate the output of f⁡(x,W(t))f(x;W^{(t)}). For the other three clusters centered at −μ1,+μ2,−μ2-\mu_{1},+\mu_{2},-\mu_{2} we have similar results, which then lead the model to generalization. Formally, we have the following theorem on generalization.

Theorem 4.8.

Suppose that Assumptions (A1)-(A6) hold. Under a good run, for C​n10​ε≤t≤nCn^{10\varepsilon}\leq t\leq\sqrt{n}, the generalization error of classifier sgn⁡(f⁡(x,W(t)))\operatorname{sgn}(f(x,W^{(t)})) has an upper bound

ℙ(x,y)∼Pclean​(y≠sgn⁡(f⁡(x,W(t))))≤exp⁡(−Ω⁡(n1−20​ε​‖μ‖4p)).\mathbb{P}_{(x,y)\sim P_{\text{clean}}}(y\neq\operatorname{sgn}(f(x;W^{(t)})))\leq\exp\left(-\Omega\left(\frac{n^{1-20\varepsilon}\|\mu\|^{4}}{p}\right)\right).

5 Discussion

We have shown that two-layer neural networks trained on XOR cluster data with random label noise by GD reveal a number of interesting phenomena. First, early in training, the network interpolates all of the training data but fails to generalize to test data better than random chance, displaying a familiar form of (catastrophic) overfitting. Later in training, the network continues to achieve a perfect fit to the noisy training data but groks useful features so that it can achieve near-zero error on test data, thus exhibiting both grokking and benign overfitting simultaneously. Notably, this provides an example of benign overfitting in neural network classification for a distribution which is not linearly separable.

In contrast to prior works on grokking which found the usage of weight decay to be crucial for grokking [Liu+22, LMT23], we observe grokking without any explicit forms of regularization, revealing the significance of the implicit regularization of GD. In our setting, the catastrophic overfitting stage of grokking occurs because early in training, the network behaves similarly to a linear classifier. This linear classifier is capable of fitting the training data due to the high-dimensionality of the feature space but fails to generalize as linear classifiers are not complex enough to achieve test performance above random chance for the XOR cluster. Later in training, the network groks useful features, corresponding to the cluster means, which allow for good generalization.

There are a few natural questions for future research. First, our analysis requires an upper bound on the number of training steps due to technical reasons; it is intriguing to understand the generalization behavior as time grows to infinity. Second, our proof crucially relies upon the assumption that the training data are nearly-orthogonal which requires that the ambient dimension is large relative to the number of samples. Prior work has shown with experiments that overfitting is less benign in this setting when the dimension is small relative to the number of samples [FCB22, Fig. 2]; a precise characterization of the effect of high-dimensional data on generalization remains open.

A.1 Additional Notation

Denote the c.d.f of standard normal distribution by Φ⁡(⋅)\Phi(\cdot) and the p.d.f. of standard normal distribution by Φ′​(⋅)\Phi^{\prime}(\cdot). Denote Φ¯​(⋅)=1−Φ​(⋅)\bar{\Phi}(\cdot)=1-\Phi(\cdot). Denote the Bernoulli distribution which takes 11 with probability p∈(0,1)p\in(0,1) by Bern​(p)\text{Bern}(p). Denote the Binomial distribution with size nn and probability pp by B​(n,p)\text{B}(n,p). For a random variable XX, denote its variance by Var​(X)\text{Var}(X); and its absolute third central moment by ρ⁡(X)\rho(X).

Proof.

Before proceeding with the proof, we recall that 𝖼𝖾𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗌={±μ1,±μ2}\mathsf{centers}=\{\pm\mu_{1},\pm\mu_{2}\}. We first show that (B1) holds with large probability. To this end, fix k∈[n]k\in[n]. ℙ(|⟨ν,ξk⟩|>t∥ν∥)≤exp(−t2/2),∀t≥1{\mathbb{P}}(|\langle\nu,\xi_{k}\rangle|>t\|\nu\|)\leq\exp(-t^{2}/2),\quad\forall t\geq 1 (A.2)

where the parameter tt in both inequality will be chosen later. To show that the first inequality of (B1) holds w.h.p, we show the complement event ℱk:={maxν∈𝖼𝖾𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗌⟨ξk,ν⟩>t∥μ∥}\mathcal{F}_{k}:=\{\max_{\nu\in\mathsf{centers}}\langle\xi_{k},\nu\rangle>t\|\mu\|\} has low probability. Applying the union bound,

ℙ⁡(ℱk)≤∑ν∈{±μ1,±μ2}ℙ(|⟨ξk,ν⟩|>t∥μ∥)∵Union bound≤4exp(−t2/2)∵Inequality (A.2).\begin{split}{\mathbb{P}}(\mathcal{F}_{k})&\leq\sum_{\nu\in\{\pm\mu_{1},\pm\mu_{2}\}}{\mathbb{P}}(|\langle\xi_{k},\nu\rangle|>t\|\mu\|)\quad\because\mbox{Union bound}\\ &\leq 4\exp(-t^{2}/2)\quad\because\mbox{Inequality \eqref{ineq:4.1.2}.}\end{split}

Let δ:=n−ε\delta:=n^{-\varepsilon}. Picking t=2​log⁡(16​n/δ)t=\sqrt{2\log(16n/\delta)} in inequality (A.2) and applying the union bound again, we have

ℙ(⋃k=1nℱk)≤4nexp(−t2/2)≤δ/4.\textstyle{\mathbb{P}}(\bigcup_{k=1}^{n}\mathcal{F}_{k})\leq 4n\exp(-t^{2}/2)\leq\delta/4. (A.3)

Next, fix t1∈(0,1)t_{1}\in(0,1) and t2≥1t_{2}\geq 1 arbitrary. To show that the second inequality of (B1) holds w.h.p, we first prove an intermediate step: the complement event ℰk:={|∥xk∥2−p−∥μ∥2|>pt1+2∥μ∥t2}{\mathcal{E}}_{k}:=\{|\|x_{k}\|^{2}-p-\|\mu\|^{2}|>pt_{1}+2\|\mu\|t_{2}\} has low probability. Towards this, first note that since

‖xk‖2=‖x¯k‖2+‖ξk‖2+2​⟨x¯k,ξk⟩=‖μ‖2+‖ξk‖2+2​⟨x¯k,ξk⟩\|x_{k}\|^{2}=\|\bar{x}_{k}\|^{2}+\|\xi_{k}\|^{2}+2\langle\bar{x}_{k},\xi_{k}\rangle=\|\mu\|^{2}+\|\xi_{k}\|^{2}+2\langle\bar{x}_{k},\xi_{k}\rangle

we have the alternative characterization of ℰk{\mathcal{E}}_{k} as

ℰk={|∥ξk∥2−p+2⟨x¯k,ξk⟩|>pt1+2∥μ∥t2}.{\mathcal{E}}_{k}=\{|\|\xi_{k}\|^{2}-p+2\langle\bar{x}_{k},\xi_{k}\rangle|>pt_{1}+2\|\mu\|t_{2}\}.

Next, recall the fact: if X,Y∈ℝX,Y\in\mathbb{R} are random variables and a,b∈ℝa,b\in\mathbb{R} are constants, then

ℙ⁡(|X+Y|>a+b)≤ℙ⁡(|X|>a)+ℙ⁡(|Y|>b).{\mathbb{P}}(|X+Y|>a+b)\leq{\mathbb{P}}(|X|>a)+{\mathbb{P}}(|Y|>b). (A.4)

≤ℙ(|∥ξk∥2−p|>pt1)+ℙ(|⟨x¯k,ξk⟩|>t2∥μ∥)∵Inequality (A.4)\displaystyle\leq{\mathbb{P}}\big(\big|\|\xi_{k}\|^{2}-p\big|>pt_{1}\big)+{\mathbb{P}}(|\langle\bar{x}_{k},\xi_{k}\rangle|>t_{2}\|\mu\|)\quad\because\mbox{Inequality \eqref{equation:lemma.4.1.simplefact}}
≤2exp(−pt12/8)+exp(−t22/2).∵Inequalities (A.1) and (A.2)\displaystyle\leq 2\exp(-pt_{1}^{2}/8)+\exp(-t_{2}^{2}/2).\quad\because\mbox{Inequalities \eqref{ineq:4.1.1} and \eqref{ineq:4.1.2}} (A.5)

Inequality (A.5) is the crucial intermediate step to proving the second inequality of (B1). It will be convenient to complete the proof of the second inequality of (B1) simultaneously with that of (B2). To this end, we next prove an analogous intermediate step to (B2).

Fix s1,s2≥1s_{1},s_{2}\geq 1 to be chosen later. ≤ℙ⁡(|ξi⊤​ξj|>s1​p)+ℙ⁡(|ξi⊤​x¯j|>t2​‖μ‖)+ℙ⁡(|ξj⊤​x¯i|>t2​‖μ‖)\displaystyle\leq{\mathbb{P}}(|\xi_{i}^{\top}\xi_{j}|>s_{1}\sqrt{p})+{\mathbb{P}}(|\xi_{i}^{\top}\bar{x}_{j}|>t_{2}\|\mu\|)+{\mathbb{P}}(|\xi_{j}^{\top}\bar{x}_{i}|>t_{2}\|\mu\|)
≤exp(−s12/2s2)+2exp(−p(s2−1)2/8)+2exp(−t22/2),\displaystyle\leq\exp(-s_{1}^{2}/2s_{2})+2\exp(-p(s_{2}-1)^{2}/8)+2\exp(-t_{2}^{2}/2), (A.6)

Moreover, ℙ⁡(|ξi⊤​x¯j|>t2​‖μ‖){\mathbb{P}}(|\xi_{i}^{\top}\bar{x}_{j}|>t_{2}\|\mu\|) and ℙ(|ξj⊤x¯i|>t2∥μ∥)≤exp(−t22/2){\mathbb{P}}(|\xi_{j}^{\top}\bar{x}_{i}|>t_{2}\|\mu\|)\leq\exp(-t_{2}^{2}/2) follows from (A.2). To prove the claim, it remains to prove

ℙ⁡(|⟨ξi,ξj⟩|>s1​p)\displaystyle{\mathbb{P}}(|\langle\xi_{i},\xi_{j}\rangle|>s_{1}\sqrt{p})
≤ℙ(|⟨ξi,ξj⟩|>s1p|∥ξj∥≤s2​p)+ℙ(∥ξj∥>s2​p)∵law of total expectation\displaystyle\leq{\mathbb{P}}\big(|\langle\xi_{i},\xi_{j}\rangle|>s_{1}\sqrt{p}\,\,\big|\,\,\|\xi_{j}\|\leq\sqrt{s_{2}p}\big)+{\mathbb{P}}(\|\xi_{j}\|>\sqrt{s_{2}p})\quad\because\mbox{law of total expectation}
≤exp(−s12/2s2)+2exp(−p(s2−1)2/8).\displaystyle\leq\exp(-s_{1}^{2}/2s_{2})+2\exp(-p(s_{2}-1)^{2}/8). (A.7)

For upper bounding the first summand, first let ℙ⁡(|⟨ξi,ξj⟩|>s1​p|ξj){\mathbb{P}}\big(|\langle\xi_{i},\xi_{j}\rangle|>s_{1}\sqrt{p}\,\,\big|\,\,\xi_{j}\big) be the conditional probability conditioned on a realization of ξj\xi_{j} (while ξi\xi_{i} remains random). Then by definition

(A.8)

For fixed ξj\xi_{j} such that ‖ξj‖≤s2​p\|\xi_{j}\|\leq\sqrt{s_{2}p}, we have by (A.2) that

ℙ(|⟨ξi,ξj⟩|>s1p|ξj)=ℙ(|⟨ξi,ξj⟩|>∥ξj∥(s1p/∥ξj∥)|ξj)≤exp(−(s1p/∥ξj∥)2/2).{\mathbb{P}}\big(|\langle\xi_{i},\xi_{j}\rangle|>s_{1}\sqrt{p}\,\,\big|\,\,\xi_{j}\big)={\mathbb{P}}\big(|\langle\xi_{i},\xi_{j}\rangle|>{\|\xi_{j}\|}(s_{1}\sqrt{p}/{\|\xi_{j}\|})\,\,\big|\,\,\xi_{j}\big)\leq\exp(-(s_{1}\sqrt{p}/{\|\xi_{j}\|})^{2}/2).

exp(−(s1p/∥ξj∥)2/2)≤exp(−(s1/s2)2/2).\exp(-(s_{1}\sqrt{p}/{\|\xi_{j}\|})^{2}/2)\leq\exp(-(s_{1}/\sqrt{s_{2}})^{2}/2).

Hence, ℙ(|⟨ξi,ξj⟩|>s1p|ξj)≤exp(−s12/2s2){\mathbb{P}}\big(|\langle\xi_{i},\xi_{j}\rangle|>s_{1}\sqrt{p}\,\,\big|\,\,\xi_{j}\big)\leq\exp(-s_{1}^{2}/2s_{2}). We now choose the values for t1=8​log⁡(16​n/δ)/pt_{1}=\sqrt{8\log(16n/\delta)/p}, t2=2​log⁡(16​n2/δ)t_{2}=\sqrt{2\log(16n^{2}/\delta)}, s1=2​log⁡(8​n2/δ)s_{1}=2\sqrt{\log(8n^{2}/\delta)}, and s2=1+8​log⁡(16​n2/δ)/p.s_{2}=1+\sqrt{8\log(16n^{2}/\delta)/p}. by Assumptions (A1) and (A2). Combining (A.5) and (A.6) then applying the union bound, we have

ℙ((∪k=1nℰk)∪(∪i,j∈[n]:i≠jℰi​j))≤∑k=1nℙ(ℰk)+∑i,j∈[n]:i≠jℙ(ℰi​j)≤2​n​exp⁡(−p​t128)+n2​[2​exp⁡(−t222)+exp⁡(−s122​s2)+2​exp⁡(−p​(s2−1)28)]≤δ.\begin{split}\textstyle{\mathbb{P}}&((\cup_{k=1}^{n}{\mathcal{E}}_{k})\cup(\cup_{i,j\in[n]:i\neq j}{\mathcal{E}}_{ij}))\leq\textstyle\sum_{k=1}^{n}{\mathbb{P}}({\mathcal{E}}_{k})+\sum_{i,j\in[n]:i\neq j}{\mathbb{P}}({\mathcal{E}}_{ij})\\ &\leq 2n\exp(-\tfrac{pt_{1}^{2}}{8})+n^{2}[2\exp(-\tfrac{t_{2}^{2}}{2})+\exp(-\tfrac{s_{1}^{2}}{2s_{2}})+2\exp(-\tfrac{p(s_{2}-1)^{2}}{8})]\leq\delta.\end{split} (A.9)

Moreover, plugging the above values of t1t_{1}, t2t_{2} and s1s_{1} into the definition of ℰk{\mathcal{E}}_{k} and ℰi​j{\mathcal{E}}_{ij}, we see that (B1) and (B2) are satisfied since they contain the complement of the event in (A.9).

Next, show that (B3) holds with large probability. We prove the inequality involving |cν+nν−n/4||c_{\nu}+n_{\nu}-n/4| portion of (B3). Proofs for the rest of the inequalities in (B3) follow analogously using the same technique below. Recall from the data generation model, for each k∈[n]k\in[n], x¯k\bar{x}_{k} is sampled  i.i.d∼Unif​{±μ1,±μ2}\text{ i.i.d}\sim\text{Unif}\{\pm\mu_{1},\pm\mu_{2}\}. Define the following indicator random variable:

𝕀ν​(k)={1if ​x¯k=ν0otherwise,for each ​k∈[n], and ​ν∈{±μ1,±μ2}\mathbb{I}_{\nu}(k)=\begin{cases}1&\text{if }\bar{x}_{k}=\nu\\ 0&\text{otherwise,}\end{cases}\quad\mbox{for each }k\in[n],\mbox{ and }\nu\in\{\pm\mu_{1},\pm\mu_{2}\}

Then we have ∑ν𝕀μ​(k)=1\sum_{\nu}\mathbb{I}_{\mu}(k)=1 for each kk, and 𝔼⁡[𝕀ν​(k)]=n/4{\mathbb{E}}[\mathbb{I}_{\nu}(k)]=n/4 for each ν\nu. Applying Hoeffding’s inequality, we obtain

ℙ⁡(|∑k=1n𝕀ν​(k)−n/4|>t​n)≤2​exp⁡(−2​t2).\textstyle{\mathbb{P}}(|\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbb{I}_{\nu}(k)-n/4|>t\sqrt{n})\leq 2\exp(-2t^{2}).

Applying the union bound, we have

ℙ⁡(maxν⁡|∑k=1n𝕀ν​(k)−n/4|>t​n)≤8​exp⁡(−2​t2).\textstyle{\mathbb{P}}(\max_{\nu}|\sum_{k=1}^{n}\mathbb{I}_{\nu}(k)-n/4|>t\sqrt{n})\leq 8\exp(-2t^{2}). (A.10)

Thus we can bound the above tail probability by O⁡(δ)O(\delta) by letting t=log⁡(1/δ)/2t=\sqrt{\log(1/\delta)/2}, and the upper bound t​n≤n​log⁡(1/δ)=n​ε​log⁡(n)t\sqrt{n}\leq\sqrt{n\log(1/\delta)}=\sqrt{n\varepsilon\log(n)}.

Next, show that (B4) holds with large probability. We prove the inequality involving |cν+nν−c−ν−n−ν||c_{\nu}+n_{\nu}-c_{-\nu}-n_{-\nu}| portion of (B4). Proofs for the rest of the inequalities in (B4) follow analogously using the same technique below. Note that for each kk,

𝔼⁡[𝕀ν​(k)−𝕀−ν​(k)]=0;𝔼⁡[|𝕀ν​(k)−𝕀−ν​(k)|l]=14​ for any ​l≥1.{\mathbb{E}}[\mathbb{I}_{\nu}(k)-\mathbb{I}_{-\nu}(k)]=0;\quad{\mathbb{E}}[|\mathbb{I}_{\nu}(k)-\mathbb{I}_{-\nu}(k)|^{l}]=\frac{1}{4}\text{ for any }l\geq 1.

It yields that

ρ⁡(𝕀ν​(k)−𝕀−ν​(k))/Var​(𝕀ν​(k)−𝕀−ν​(k))3/2=2.\rho(\mathbb{I}_{\nu}(k)-\mathbb{I}_{-\nu}(k))/\text{Var}(\mathbb{I}_{\nu}(k)-\mathbb{I}_{-\nu}(k))^{3/2}=2.

Applying the Berry-Esseen theorem (Lemma A.19), we have

ℙ⁡(|cν+nν−c−ν−n−ν|>t​n)=ℙ⁡(|∑k=1n(𝕀ν​(k)−𝕀−ν​(k))|>t​n)≥2​Φ¯​(2​t)−12n.{\mathbb{P}}(|c_{\nu}+n_{\nu}-c_{-\nu}-n_{-\nu}|>t\sqrt{n})={\mathbb{P}}(|\sum_{k=1}^{n}(\mathbb{I}_{\nu}(k)-\mathbb{I}_{-\nu}(k))|>t\sqrt{n})\geq 2\bar{\Phi}(2t)-\frac{12}{\sqrt{n}}.

Let t=n−εt=n^{-\varepsilon}. By Φ⁡(t)≤1/2+Φ′​(0)​t\Phi(t)\leq 1/2+\Phi^{\prime}(0)t, we have

ℙ⁡(|∑k=1n(𝕀ν​(k)−𝕀−ν​(k))|>t​n)≥1−42​π​nε−12n=1−O⁡(δ).{\mathbb{P}}(|\sum_{k=1}^{n}(\mathbb{I}_{\nu}(k)-\mathbb{I}_{-\nu}(k))|>t\sqrt{n})\geq 1-\frac{4}{\sqrt{2\pi}n^{\varepsilon}}-\frac{12}{\sqrt{n}}=1-O(\delta). (A.11)

Combining (A.3), (A.9)-(A.11), we prove that conditions (B1)-(B4) hold with probability at least 1−O⁡(δ)1-O(\delta) over the randomness of the training data. As a consequence of (B1), we have

p/2≤p+‖μ‖2−10​p​log⁡(n)≤‖xk‖2≤p+‖μ‖2+10​p​log⁡(n)≤2​pp/2\leq p+\|\mu\|^{2}-10\sqrt{p\log(n)}\leq\|x_{k}\|^{2}\leq p+\|\mu\|^{2}+10\sqrt{p\log(n)}\leq 2p

by Assumption (A1) and (A2). ∎

A.2.2 Proof of Corollary 4.2

See 4.2

Proof.

By Lemma 4.1, we have that under (B1) and (B2), when i≠ji\neq j,

|⟨xi,xj⟩|‖xi‖⋅‖xj‖≤‖μ‖2+10​p​log⁡(n)p+‖μ‖2−10​p​log⁡(n)≤2​‖μ‖2p≤2C​n2,\frac{|\langle x_{i},x_{j}\rangle|}{\|x_{i}\|\cdot\|x_{j}\|}\leq\frac{\|\mu\|^{2}+10\sqrt{p\log(n)}}{p+\|\mu\|^{2}-10\sqrt{p\log(n)}}\leq\frac{2\|\mu\|^{2}}{p}\leq\frac{2}{Cn^{2}},

for sufficiently large pp. Here the second inequality comes from Assumption (A1); and the last inequality comes from Assumption (A2). ∎

A.3 Properties of the initial weights and activation patterns

We begin with additional notations that is used for the proofs of Lemmas 4.3 and 4.4. Following the notations in [XG23], we simplify the notation of 𝒥𝙿𝚘𝚜\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Pos}}} and 𝒥𝙽𝚎𝚐\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Neg}}} defined in Section 4 as

𝒥𝙿:=𝒥𝙿𝚘𝚜={j∈[m]:aj>0};𝒥𝙽:=𝒥𝙽𝚎𝚐={j∈[m]:aj<0}.\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{P}}}:=\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Pos}}}=\{j\in[m]:a_{j}>0\};\quad\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{N}}}:=\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Neg}}}=\{j\in[m]:a_{j}<0\}.

We denote the set of pairs (i,j)(i,j) such that the neuron jj is active with respect to the sample xix_{i} at time tt by 𝒜(t){\mathcal{A}}^{(t)}, i.e., define

𝒜(t):={(i,j)∈[n]×[m]:⟨wj(t),xi⟩>0}.\mathcal{A}^{(t)}:=\{(i,j)\in[n]\times[m]:\langle w_{j}^{(t)},x_{i}\rangle>0\}.

Define subsets 𝒜i,(t)\mathcal{A}^{i,(t)} and 𝒜j(t)\mathcal{A}_{j}^{(t)} of 𝒜(t){\mathcal{A}}^{(t)} where ii (resp. jj) is a sample (resp. neuron) index:

𝒜i,(t):={j∈[m]:⟨wj(t),xi⟩>0},\mathcal{A}^{i,(t)}:=\{j\in[m]:\langle w_{j}^{(t)},x_{i}\rangle>0\},
𝒜j(t):={i∈[n]:⟨wj(t),xi⟩>0}.\mathcal{A}_{j}^{(t)}:=\{i\in[n]:\langle w_{j}^{(t)},x_{i}\rangle>0\}.

Define

𝒞ν,j(t)=𝒞ν∩𝒜j(t);𝒩ν,j(t)=𝒩ν∩𝒜j(t), for ​j∈[m],ν∈𝖼𝖾𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗌.\mathcal{C}_{\nu,j}^{(t)}={\mathcal{C}}_{\nu}\cap{\mathcal{A}}_{j}^{(t)};\quad\mathcal{N}_{\nu,j}^{(t)}={\mathcal{N}}_{\nu}\cap{\mathcal{A}}_{j}^{(t)},\text{ for }j\in[m],\nu\in\mathsf{centers}.

Note that the above definition is equivalent to (4.1) from the main text.

Let n±ν:=nν+n−νn_{\pm\nu}:=n_{\nu}+n_{-\nu}. For ν∈𝖼𝖾𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗌\nu\in\mathsf{centers}, we denote the sets of indices jj of (ν,κ)(\nu,\kappa)-aligned neurons (see (4.2) in the main text for the definition of (ν,κ)(\nu,\kappa)-aligned-ness) with parameter κ∈[0,12)\kappa\in[0,\tfrac{1}{2}):

𝒥νκ:={j∈[m]:Dν,j(0)>n1/2−κ,andd−ν,j(0)<min{cν,c−ν}−2n±ν−n}.\mathcal{J}_{\nu}^{\kappa}:=\{j\in[m]:D_{\nu,j}^{(0)}>n^{1/2-\kappa},\,\,\mbox{and}\,\,d_{-\nu,j}^{(0)}<\min\{c_{\nu},c_{-\nu}\}-2n_{\pm\nu}-\sqrt{n}\}.

Thus, we have by definition that

𝒥νκ={j∈𝒥𝙿:neuron j is (ν,κ)-aligned}\mathcal{J}_{\nu}^{\kappa}=\{j\in\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{P}}}:\mbox{neuron $j$ is $(\nu,\kappa)$-aligned}\}

Further we denote

𝒥𝙿i,(t)=𝒥𝙿∩𝒜i,(t);𝒥𝙽i,(t)=𝒥𝙽∩𝒜i,(t).\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{P}}}^{i,(t)}=\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{P}}}\cap\mathcal{A}^{i,(t)};\quad\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{N}}}^{i,(t)}=\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{N}}}\cap\mathcal{A}^{i,(t)}. (A.12)

Finally, we denote

𝒥ν,𝙿κ=𝒥𝙿∩𝒥νκ;𝒥ν,𝙽κ=𝒥𝙽∩𝒥νκ.\displaystyle\mathcal{J}_{\nu,{\mathtt{P}}}^{\kappa}=\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{P}}}\cap\mathcal{J}_{\nu}^{\kappa};\quad\mathcal{J}_{\nu,{\mathtt{N}}}^{\kappa}=\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{N}}}\cap\mathcal{J}_{\nu}^{\kappa}. (A.13)

A.3.1 Proof of Lemma 4.3

See 4.3

Proof.

Recall earlier for simplicity, we defined for simplicity 𝒥𝙿=𝒥𝙿𝚘𝚜\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{P}}}=\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Pos}}} and 𝒥𝙽=𝒥𝙽𝚎𝚐\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{N}}}=\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{Neg}}}. Let δ=n−ε\delta=n^{-\varepsilon}. Then (C1) is proved to hold with probability 1−O⁡(δ)1-O(\delta) in the Lemma 4.2 of [FCB22a]. For (C2), since |𝒥𝙿||\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{P}}}| and |𝒥𝙽||\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{N}}}| both follow distribution B​(m,1/2)\text{B}(m,1/2), it suffices to show that ℙ⁡(|𝒥𝙿|≥m/3)≥1−δ{\mathbb{P}}(|\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{P}}}|\geq m/3)\geq 1-\delta. Applying Hoeffding’s inequality, we have

ℙ(|𝒥𝙿|≤m/3)=ℙ(|𝒥𝙿|−m/2≤−m/6)≤exp(−m/18)≤δ,{\mathbb{P}}(|\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{P}}}|\leq m/3)={\mathbb{P}}(|\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{P}}}|-m/2\leq-m/6)\leq\exp(-m/18)\leq\delta,

where the last inequality comes from Assumption (A6). ∎

|⟨wj(t+1)−wj(t),ν⟩−α​aj2​n​yν​Dν,j(t)​‖μ‖2|≤5​αn3/2​m​‖μ‖2.\displaystyle\Big|\langle w_{j}^{(t+1)}-w_{j}^{(t)},\nu\rangle-\frac{\alpha a_{j}}{2n}y_{\nu}D_{\nu,j}^{(t)}\|\mu\|^{2}\Big|\leq\frac{5\alpha}{n^{3/2}\sqrt{m}}\|\mu\|^{2}. (A.29)

where Cn:=10​log⁡(n)C_{n}:=10\sqrt{\log(n)}, x¯k∈𝖼𝖾𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗌\bar{x}_{k}\in\mathsf{centers} is defined as the cluster mean for sample (xk,yk)(x_{k},y_{k}), and yνy_{\nu} is defined as the clean label for cluster centered at ν\nu (i.e. yν=1y_{\nu}=1 for ν∈{±μ1}\nu\in\{\pm\mu_{1}\}, yν=−1y_{\nu}=-1 for ν∈{±μ2}\nu\in\{\pm\mu_{2}\}).

Taking a closer look at (A.28), we see that if aj​yk>0a_{j}y_{k}>0, and xkx_{k} activates neuron wjw_{j} at time ss, then xkx_{k} will activate neuron wj(t)w_{j}^{(t)} for any t∈[s,1/(n​p​α)−2]t\in[s,1/(\sqrt{n}p\alpha)-2]. Moreover, if aj​yk<0a_{j}y_{k}<0, and xkx_{k} activates neuron wjw_{j} at time ss, then xkx_{k} will not activate neuron wjw_{j} at time s+1s+1, which implies that there is an upper bound for the inner product ⟨wj(t),xk⟩\langle w_{j}^{(t)},x_{k}\rangle. These observations are stated as the corollary below:

Corollary A.5.

Suppose that Assumptions (A1)-(A6) hold. Under a good run, for any pair (j,k)∈[m]×[n](j,k)\in[m]\times[n], the following is true:

  1. (E1)

    When aj​yk>0a_{j}y_{k}>0, if there exists some 0≤s<1/(n​p​α)−20\leq s<1/(\sqrt{n}p\alpha)-2 such that ⟨wj(s),xk⟩>0\langle w_{j}^{(s)},x_{k}\rangle>0, then for any s≤t≤1/(n​p​α)−2s\leq t\leq 1/(\sqrt{n}p\alpha)-2, we have ⟨wj(t),xk⟩>0\langle w_{j}^{(t)},x_{k}\rangle>0.

  2. (E2)

    When aj​yk<0a_{j}y_{k}<0, for any 0≤t≤1/(n​p​α)−20\leq t\leq 1/(\sqrt{n}p\alpha)-2, we have that ⟨wj(t),xk⟩≤αm​‖μ‖2.\langle w_{j}^{(t)},x_{k}\rangle\leq\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{m}}\|\mu\|^{2}.

  3. (E3)

    When aj​yk<0a_{j}y_{k}<0, for any 0≤t≤1/(n​p​α)−30\leq t\leq 1/(\sqrt{n}p\alpha)-3, we have that ⟨wj(t),xk⟩>0\langle w_{j}^{(t)},x_{k}\rangle>0 implies ⟨wj(t+1),xk⟩<0.\langle w_{j}^{(t+1)},x_{k}\rangle<0.

A.5 Proof of the Main Theorem

We rigorously prove Theorem 3.1 in this section. The upper bound of tt in the theorems below is 1/(n​p​α)−21/(\sqrt{n}p\alpha)-2, which by Assumption (A4), is larger than n\sqrt{n}, the upper bound of tt in Theorem 3.1.

A.5.1 Proof of Theorem A.8: 1-step Overfitting

Theorem A.8.

Suppose that Assumptions (A1)-(A6) hold. Under a good run, the classifier sgn⁡(f⁡(x,W(t)))\operatorname{sgn}(f(x,W^{(t)})) can correctly classify all training datapoints for 1≤t≤1/(n​p​α)−21\leq t\leq 1/(\sqrt{n}p\alpha)-2.

Proof.

Without loss of generality, we only consider datapoints in the cluster 𝒞+μ1∪𝒩+μ1{\mathcal{C}}_{+\mu_{1}}\cup{\mathcal{N}}_{+\mu_{1}}. According to (D1) in Lemma 4.4, we have that under a good run, |𝒥𝙿i,(0)|≥m/7,|𝒥𝙽i,(0)|≥m/7|\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{P}}}^{i,(0)}|\geq m/7,|\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{N}}}^{i,(0)}|\geq m/7 for each i∈[n]i\in[n]. For xk∈𝒞+μ1x_{k}\in{\mathcal{C}}_{+\mu_{1}}, by Corollary A.5, we have

⟨wj(s),xk⟩>0\langle w_{j}^{(s)},x_{k}\rangle>0

for all j∈𝒥𝙿k,(0)j\in\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{P}}}^{k,(0)} and 0≤s≤1/(n​p​α)−20\leq s\leq 1/(\sqrt{n}p\alpha)-2; and

⟨wj(s),xk⟩≤αm​‖μ‖2\langle w_{j}^{(s)},x_{k}\rangle\leq\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{m}}\|\mu\|^{2}

for all j∈𝒥𝙽j\in\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{N}}} and 0≤s≤1/(n​p​α)−20\leq s\leq 1/(\sqrt{n}p\alpha)-2. Then for 1≤t≤1/(n​p​α)−21\leq t\leq 1/(\sqrt{n}p\alpha)-2, we have

∑j=1maj​ϕ​(⟨wj(t),xk⟩)≥∑j∈𝒥𝙿k,(0)1mϕ(⟨wj(t),xk⟩)−∑j:aj<01mϕ(⟨wj(t),xk⟩)≥∑j∈𝒥𝙿k,(0)∑s=0t−11m⟨wj(s+1)−wj(s),xk⟩−∑j:aj<0αm∥μ∥2≥α​p​t4​n​m​|𝒥𝙿k,(0)|−α​|𝒥𝙽|m​‖μ‖2≥α​p​t28​n−α​‖μ‖2>0,\begin{split}\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_{j}\phi(\langle w_{j}^{(t)},x_{k}\rangle)&\geq\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{P}}}^{k,(0)}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\phi(\langle w_{j}^{(t)},x_{k}\rangle)-\sum_{j:a_{j}<0}\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\phi(\langle w_{j}^{(t)},x_{k}\rangle)\\ &\geq\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{P}}}^{k,(0)}}\sum_{s=0}^{t-1}\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\langle w_{j}^{(s+1)}-w_{j}^{(s)},x_{k}\rangle-\sum_{j:a_{j}<0}\frac{\alpha}{m}\|\mu\|^{2}\\ &\geq\frac{\alpha pt}{4nm}|\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{P}}}^{k,(0)}|-\frac{\alpha|\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{N}}}|}{m}\|\mu\|^{2}\\ &\geq\frac{\alpha pt}{28n}-\alpha\|\mu\|^{2}>0,\end{split}

where the first inequality uses ϕ⁡(x)≥0,∀x\phi(x)\geq 0,\forall x; the second inequality uses the definition of 𝒥𝙿k,(0)\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{P}}}^{k,(0)} and (E2) in Corollary A.5; the third inequality uses (A.35) in Corollary A.5; and the last inequality is from Assumption (A2). For xk∈𝒩+μ1x_{k}\in{\mathcal{N}}_{+\mu_{1}}, similarly we have

∑j=1maj​ϕ​(⟨wj(t),xk⟩)≤−∑j∈𝒥𝙽k,(0)1mϕ(⟨wj(t),xk⟩)+∑j:aj>01mϕ(⟨wj(t),xk⟩)≤−∑j∈𝒥𝙽k,(0)∑s=1t1m⟨wj(s)−wj(s−1),xk⟩+∑j:aj>0αm∥μ∥2≤−(α​p​t28​n−α​‖μ‖2)<0.\begin{split}\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_{j}\phi(\langle w_{j}^{(t)},x_{k}\rangle)&\leq-\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{N}}}^{k,(0)}}\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\phi(\langle w_{j}^{(t)},x_{k}\rangle)+\sum_{j:a_{j}>0}\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\phi(\langle w_{j}^{(t)},x_{k}\rangle)\\ &\leq-\sum_{j\in\mathcal{J}_{{\mathtt{N}}}^{k,(0)}}\sum_{s=1}^{t}\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\langle w_{j}^{(s)}-w_{j}^{(s-1)},x_{k}\rangle+\sum_{j:a_{j}>0}\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt{m}}\|\mu\|^{2}\\ &\leq-(\frac{\alpha pt}{28n}-\alpha\|\mu\|^{2})<0.\end{split}

Thus our classifier can correctly classify all training datapoints for 1≤t≤1/(n​p​α)−21\leq t\leq 1/(\sqrt{n}p\alpha)-2. ∎

A.5.2 Proof of Theorem 4.8: Generalization

Before proceeding with the proof of Theorem 4.8, we first state a technical lemma:

Lemma A.9.

Suppose that ‖W‖>0\|W\|>0. Then there exists a constant c>0c>0 such that

ℙ(x,y~)∼Pclean​(y~≠sgn⁡(f⁡(x,W)))≤maxν∈𝖼𝖾𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗌⁡2​exp⁡(−c​(𝔼x∼N⁡(ν,Ip)​[f​(x,W)]‖W‖F)2).\mathbb{P}_{(x,\widetilde{y})\sim P_{\text{clean}}}(\widetilde{y}\neq\operatorname{sgn}(f(x;W)))\leq\max_{\nu\in\mathsf{centers}}2\exp\left(-c\left(\frac{{\mathbb{E}}_{x\sim N(\nu,I_{p})}[f(x;W)]}{\|W\|_{F}}\right)^{2}\right).
Proof.

It suffices to prove that for each ν∈𝖼𝖾𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗌\nu\in\mathsf{centers},

ℙx∼N⁡(ν,Ip)​(yν​f​(x,W)<0)≤2​exp⁡(−c​(𝔼x∼N⁡(ν,Ip)​[f​(x,W)]‖W‖F)2).\mathbb{P}_{x\sim N(\nu,I_{p})}(y_{\nu}f(x;W)<0)\leq 2\exp\left(-c\left(\frac{{\mathbb{E}}_{x\sim N(\nu,I_{p})}[f(x;W)]}{\|W\|_{F}}\right)^{2}\right). (A.62)

Then applying the law of total expectation, we have

ℙ(x,y~)∼Pclean​(y~≠sgn⁡(f⁡(x,W)))=14​∑ν∈𝖼𝖾𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗌ℙx∼N⁡(ν,Ip)​(yν≠sgn⁡(f⁡(x,W)))≤12​∑ν∈𝖼𝖾𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗌exp⁡(−c​(𝔼x∼N⁡(ν,Ip)​[f​(x,W)]‖W‖F)2)≤maxν∈𝖼𝖾𝗇𝗍𝖾𝗋𝗌⁡2​exp⁡(−c​(𝔼x∼N⁡(ν,Ip)​[f​(x,W)]‖W‖F)2).\begin{split}\mathbb{P}_{(x,\widetilde{y})\sim P_{\text{clean}}}(\widetilde{y}\neq\operatorname{sgn}(f(x;W)))&=\frac{1}{4}\sum_{\nu\in\mathsf{centers}}\mathbb{P}_{x\sim N(\nu,I_{p})}(y_{\nu}\neq\operatorname{sgn}(f(x;W)))\\ &\leq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\nu\in\mathsf{centers}}\exp\left(-c\left(\frac{{\mathbb{E}}_{x\sim N(\nu,I_{p})}[f(x;W)]}{\|W\|_{F}}\right)^{2}\right)\\ &\leq\max_{\nu\in\mathsf{centers}}2\exp\left(-c\left(\frac{{\mathbb{E}}_{x\sim N(\nu,I_{p})}[f(x;W)]}{\|W\|_{F}}\right)^{2}\right).\end{split}

Since for each ν\nu, N⁡(ν,Ip)N(\nu,I_{p}) is 11-strongly log-concave, we plug in λ=1\lambda=1 in the proof of Lemma 4.1 in [FCB22a]. Then (A.62) is obtained.

Let zi(t)=yi​f​(xi,W(t))z_{i}^{(t)}=y_{i}f(x_{i};W^{(t)}). Note that ℓ′(z)=−1/(1+exp(z))\ell^{\prime}(z)=-1/(1+\exp(z)), we have |−ℓ′​(z)−1/2|≤|z|/2|-\ell^{\prime}(z)-1/2|\leq|z|/2. It yields that

|hi(0)|≤12​|zi(0)|≤12​∑j=1|aj​⟨wj(0),xi⟩|≤12​∑j=1maj2​∑j=1m‖wj(0)‖2⋅‖x‖2=12​‖W(0)‖F⋅‖xi‖≤12​p​ωinit​3​m,\begin{split}|h_{i}^{(0)}|&\leq\frac{1}{2}|z_{i}^{(0)}|\leq\frac{1}{2}\sum_{j=1}|a_{j}\langle w_{j}^{(0)},x_{i}\rangle|\leq\frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_{j}^{2}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\|w_{j}^{(0)}\|^{2}\cdot\|x\|^{2}}\\ &=\frac{1}{2}\|W^{(0)}\|_{F}\cdot\|x_{i}\|\leq\frac{1}{2}p\omega_{\text{init}}\sqrt{3m},\end{split} (A.73)

where the first inequality uses hi(t)=gi(t)−1/2h_{i}^{(t)}=g_{i}^{(t)}-1/2 and gi(t):=−ℓ′​(zi(t))g_{i}^{(t)}:=-\ell^{\prime}(z_{i}^{(t)}); the second inequality uses triangle inequality; the third inequality uses Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; and the last inequality uses (B1) in Lemma 4.1 and (C1) in Lemma 4.3. Denote hmax=maxi∈[n]⁡|hi(0)|h_{\max}=\max_{i\in[n]}|h_{i}^{(0)}|. Then we have

‖wj,𝚃(1)−wj(1)‖=αn​m​‖∑i=1nhi(0)​ϕ′​(⟨wj(0),xi⟩)​yi​xi‖≤α​hmaxn​m​∑i=1n‖xi‖2+n⁡(n−1)​maxi≠j​|xi⊤​xj|≤α​hmaxn​m​4​n​p≤3​α​ωinit​p3/2n,\begin{split}\|w_{j,{\mathtt{T}}}^{(1)}-w_{j}^{(1)}\|&=\frac{\alpha}{n\sqrt{m}}\|\sum_{i=1}^{n}h_{i}^{{(0)}}\phi^{\prime}(\langle w_{j}^{(0)},x_{i}\rangle)y_{i}x_{i}\|\\ &\leq\frac{\alpha h_{\max}}{n\sqrt{m}}\sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\|x_{i}\|^{2}+n(n-1)\max_{i\neq j}|x_{i}^{\top}x_{j}|}\\ &\leq\frac{\alpha h_{\max}}{n\sqrt{m}}\sqrt{4np}\leq\frac{\sqrt{3}\alpha\omega_{\text{init}}p^{3/2}}{\sqrt{n}},\end{split}

where the second inequality uses ‖xi‖2≤2​p\|x_{i}\|^{2}\leq 2p and p≥C​n2​‖μ‖2p\geq Cn^{2}\|\mu\|^{2}, which come from (B1) and (B2) in Lemma 4.1 and Assumption (A2) respectively, and the third inequality uses (A.73). Further we have

‖W𝚃(1)−W(1)‖F=∑j=1m‖wj,𝚃(1)−wj(1)‖2≤α​ωinit​p3/2​3​mn.\|W_{{\mathtt{T}}}^{(1)}-W^{(1)}\|_{F}=\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{m}\|w_{j,{\mathtt{T}}}^{(1)}-w_{j}^{(1)}\|^{2}}\leq\frac{\alpha\omega_{\text{init}}p^{3/2}\sqrt{3m}}{\sqrt{n}}.

Lemma A.11.

Suppose that Assumptions (A1)-(A6) hold. Given X∈𝒢dataX\in\mathcal{G}_{\text{data}}, for each j∈[m]j\in[m], we have

n/24≤Var​(D+μ1,j(0))≤n/2;n/24\leq\text{Var}(D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)})\leq n/2;
𝔼[|D+μ1,j(0))−𝔼[D+μ1,j(0))]|3]≤n3/2.{\mathbb{E}}\big[\big|D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)})-{\mathbb{E}}[D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)})]\big|^{3}\big]\leq n^{3/2}.
Proof.

Recall that 𝒜1=𝒞+μ1∪𝒩−μ1{\mathcal{A}}_{1}={\mathcal{C}}_{+\mu_{1}}\cup{\mathcal{N}}_{-\mu_{1}}, 𝒜2=𝒞−μ1∪𝒩+μ1{\mathcal{A}}_{2}={\mathcal{C}}_{-\mu_{1}}\cup{\mathcal{N}}_{+\mu_{1}}. According to equation (A.17), we have

D+μ1,j(0)=∑i∈𝒜1𝕀⁡(zi>0)−∑i∈𝒜2𝕀⁡(zi>0).D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)}=\sum_{i\in{\mathcal{A}}_{1}}\mathbb{I}(z_{i}>0)-\sum_{i\in{\mathcal{A}}_{2}}\mathbb{I}(z_{i}>0). (A.74)

According to Lemma A.15, we have

Var​(D+μ1,j(0))=𝔼B​[f1​(b1,⋯,bn)]≥12​𝔼B′​[f1​(b1′,⋯,bn′)]=12​VarB′​(∑i∈𝒜1bi′−∑i∈𝒜2bi′)=|𝒜1|+|𝒜2|8≥n24,\begin{split}\text{Var}(D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)})&={\mathbb{E}}_{B}[f_{1}(b_{1},\cdots,b_{n})]\geq\frac{1}{2}{\mathbb{E}}_{B^{\prime}}[f_{1}(b_{1}^{\prime},\cdots,b_{n}^{\prime})]\\ &=\frac{1}{2}\text{Var}_{B^{\prime}}(\sum_{i\in{\mathcal{A}}_{1}}b_{i}^{\prime}-\sum_{i\in{\mathcal{A}}_{2}}b_{i}^{\prime})=\frac{|{\mathcal{A}}_{1}|+|{\mathcal{A}}_{2}|}{8}\geq\frac{n}{24},\end{split}

where f1​(b1,⋯,bn):=(∑i∈𝒜1bi−∑i∈𝒜2bi−(|𝒜1|−|𝒜2|)/2)2≥0f_{1}(b_{1},\cdots,b_{n}):=(\sum_{i\in{\mathcal{A}}_{1}}b_{i}-\sum_{i\in{\mathcal{A}}_{2}}b_{i}-(|{\mathcal{A}}_{1}|-|{\mathcal{A}}_{2}|)/2)^{2}\geq 0, and bi′b_{i}^{\prime} are i.i.d Bernoulli random variables defined in Lemma A.15, and the last inequality is from (A.16). On the other side, similarly we have

Var​(D+μ1,j(0))≤2​𝔼B′​[f1​(b1′,⋯,bn′)]=(|𝒜1|+|𝒜2|)/2≤n/2,\text{Var}(D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)})\leq 2{\mathbb{E}}_{B^{\prime}}[f_{1}(b_{1}^{\prime},\cdots,b_{n}^{\prime})]=(|{\mathcal{A}}_{1}|+|{\mathcal{A}}_{2}|)/2\leq n/2, (A.75)

where the last inequality is from (B3) in Lemma 4.1. Denote f2​(b1,⋯,bn):=(∑i∈𝒜1bi−∑i∈𝒜2bi−(|𝒜1|−|𝒜2|)/2)4≥0f_{2}(b_{1},\cdots,b_{n}):=(\sum_{i\in{\mathcal{A}}_{1}}b_{i}-\sum_{i\in{\mathcal{A}}_{2}}b_{i}-(|{\mathcal{A}}_{1}|-|{\mathcal{A}}_{2}|)/2)^{4}\geq 0, then we have

𝔼⁡[|D+μ1,j(0)−𝔼⁡[D+μ1,j(0)]|4]=𝔼B​[f2​(b1,⋯,bn)]≤2​𝔼B′​[f2​(b1′,⋯,bn′)]=2​𝔼B′​[[∑i∈𝒜1(bi′−12)−∑i∈𝒜2(bi′−12)]4]≤16​𝔼B′​[[∑i∈𝒜1(bi′−12)]4+[∑i∈𝒜2(bi′−12)]4]≤4​(|𝒜1|2+|𝒜2|2)≤n2,\begin{split}{\mathbb{E}}[|D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)}-{\mathbb{E}}[D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)}]|^{4}]&={\mathbb{E}}_{B}[f_{2}(b_{1},\cdots,b_{n})]\leq 2{\mathbb{E}}_{B^{\prime}}[f_{2}(b_{1}^{\prime},\cdots,b_{n}^{\prime})]\\ &=2{\mathbb{E}}_{B^{\prime}}\big[\big[\sum_{i\in{\mathcal{A}}_{1}}(b_{i}^{\prime}-\frac{1}{2})-\sum_{i\in{\mathcal{A}}_{2}}(b_{i}^{\prime}-\frac{1}{2})\big]^{4}\big]\\ &\leq 16{\mathbb{E}}_{B^{\prime}}\big[\big[\sum_{i\in{\mathcal{A}}_{1}}(b_{i}^{\prime}-\frac{1}{2})\big]^{4}+\big[\sum_{i\in{\mathcal{A}}_{2}}(b_{i}^{\prime}-\frac{1}{2})\big]^{4}\big]\\ &\leq 4(|{\mathcal{A}}_{1}|^{2}+|{\mathcal{A}}_{2}|^{2})\leq n^{2},\end{split} (A.76)

where the first inequality uses Lemma A.15; the second inequality uses (a+b)4≤8​(a4+b4)(a+b)^{4}\leq 8(a^{4}+b^{4}); the third inequality uses the formula of the fourth central moment of a binomial distribution with parameter equal to 1/21/2, i.e. μ4​(B​(n,1/2))=n⁡(1+(3​n−6)/4)/4≤n2/4\mu_{4}(\text{B}(n,1/2))=n(1+(3n-6)/4)/4\leq n^{2}/4; and the last inequality is from (B3) in Lemma 4.1. Combining (A.75) and (A.76), we have

𝔼[|D+μ1,j(0))−𝔼[D+μ1,j(0))]|3]≤Var​(D+μ1,j(0))​𝔼​[|D+μ1,j(0)−𝔼⁡[D+μ1,j(0)]|4]≤n3/2{\mathbb{E}}\big[\big|D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)})-{\mathbb{E}}[D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)})]\big|^{3}\big]\leq\sqrt{\text{Var}(D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)}){\mathbb{E}}[|D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)}-{\mathbb{E}}[D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)}]|^{4}]}\leq n^{3/2}

by applying the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality.

Lemma A.12.

Suppose that Assumptions (A1)-(A6) hold. Given X=[x1,⋯,xn]⊤∈𝒢dataX=[x_{1},\cdots,x_{n}]^{\top}\in\mathcal{G}_{\text{data}}, we have

ℙ⁡(|∑j=1maj​ϕ​(aj​D+μ1,j(0))−12​𝔼​[D+μ1,j(0)]|>t)≤2​Φ¯​(t​m3​Cn​n​ε)+Cm;{\mathbb{P}}(\Big|\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_{j}\phi(a_{j}D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)})-\frac{1}{2}{\mathbb{E}}[D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)}]\Big|>t)\leq 2\bar{\Phi}\big(\frac{t\sqrt{m}}{3C_{n}\sqrt{n\varepsilon}}\big)+\frac{C}{\sqrt{m}};
ℙ⁡(|∑j=1maj​|aj​D+μ1,j(0)||>t)≤2​Φ¯​(t​m3​Cn​n​ε)+Cm.{\mathbb{P}}(\Big|\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_{j}|a_{j}D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)}|\Big|>t)\leq 2\bar{\Phi}\big(\frac{t\sqrt{m}}{3C_{n}\sqrt{n\varepsilon}}\big)+\frac{C}{\sqrt{m}}.
Proof.

In this proof, by convention all ℙ⁡(⋅),𝔼⁡[⋅],Var​(⋅),ρ⁡(⋅){\mathbb{P}}(\cdot),{\mathbb{E}}[\cdot],\text{Var}(\cdot),\rho(\cdot) are implicitly conditioned on a fixed XX. Denote the expectation of D+μ1,j(0)D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)} by e+μ1e_{+\mu_{1}}. Note that conditioning on XX, {aj​ϕ​(aj​D+μ1,j(0))}j≥1\{a_{j}\phi(a_{j}D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)})\}_{j\geq 1} are i.i.d, and the expectation of D+μ1,j(0)D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)} is

e+μ1=(c+μ1−n+μ1−c−μ1+n−μ1)/2≤2​Cn​n​ε,e_{+\mu_{1}}=(c_{+\mu_{1}}-n_{+\mu_{1}}-c_{-\mu_{1}}+n_{-\mu_{1}})/2\leq 2C_{n}\sqrt{n\varepsilon}, (A.77)

where the inequality uses (B3) in Lemma 4.1. By Lemma A.11, we have

n24≤Var​(D+μ1,j(0))≤n2;ρ⁡(D+μ1,j(0))≤n3/2.\frac{n}{24}\leq\text{Var}\big(D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)}\big)\leq\frac{n}{2};\quad\rho(D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)})\leq n^{3/2}. (A.78)

Denote

σ+μ12=Var​(m​aj​ϕ​(aj​D+μ1,j(0)));ρ+μ1=ρ⁡(m​aj​ϕ​(aj​D+μ1,j(0))).\sigma_{+\mu_{1}}^{2}=\text{Var}\big(ma_{j}\phi(a_{j}D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)})\big);\quad\rho_{+\mu_{1}}=\rho(ma_{j}\phi(a_{j}D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)})).

Combining (A.78) and results in Lemma A.14, we have

𝔼⁡[m​aj​ϕ​(aj​D+μ1,j(0))]=e+μ12;max⁡{n48,e+μ124}≤σ+μ12≤max⁡{n2,e+μ122};ρ+μ1≤32​max​{n3/2,|e+μ1|3}.{\mathbb{E}}[ma_{j}\phi(a_{j}D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)})]=\frac{e_{+\mu_{1}}}{2};\quad\max\{\frac{n}{48},\frac{e_{+\mu_{1}}^{2}}{4}\}\leq\sigma_{+\mu_{1}}^{2}\leq\max\{\frac{n}{2},\frac{e_{+\mu_{1}}^{2}}{2}\};\quad\rho_{+\mu_{1}}\leq 32\max\{n^{3/2},|e_{+\mu_{1}}|^{3}\}. (A.79)

Applying Berry-Esseen theorem, we have

ℙ⁡(|∑j=1maj​ϕ​(aj​D+μ1,j(0))−12​e+μ1|>t)≤2​Φ¯​(t​mσ+μ1)+CBE​ρ+μ1σ+μ13​m≤2​Φ¯​(t​mn+2​Cn​n​ε)+Cm{\mathbb{P}}(\Big|\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_{j}\phi(a_{j}D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)})-\frac{1}{2}e_{+\mu_{1}}\Big|>t)\leq 2\bar{\Phi}\big(\frac{t\sqrt{m}}{\sigma_{+\mu_{1}}}\big)+\frac{C_{\text{BE}}\rho_{+\mu_{1}}}{\sigma_{+\mu_{1}}^{3}\sqrt{m}}\leq 2\bar{\Phi}\big(\frac{t\sqrt{m}}{\sqrt{n}+2C_{n}\sqrt{n\varepsilon}}\big)+\frac{C}{\sqrt{m}}

for some universal constant C>0C>0. Here the second inequality uses σ+μ12≤(n+|e+μ1|)2\sigma_{+\mu_{1}}^{2}\leq(\sqrt{n}+|e_{+\mu_{1}}|)^{2}, which comes from (A.79), and the last inequality uses (A.77). By the symmetry of aja_{j}, we have

𝔼⁡[m​aj​|aj​D+μ1,j(0)|]=0;Var​(m​aj​|aj​D+μ1,j(0)|)=𝔼⁡[(D+μ1,j(0))2];ρ⁡(m​aj​|aj​D+μ1,j(0)|)=𝔼⁡[|D+μ1,j(0)|3].{\mathbb{E}}[ma_{j}|a_{j}D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)}|]=0;\quad\text{Var}(ma_{j}|a_{j}D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)}|)={\mathbb{E}}[(D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)})^{2}];\quad\rho(ma_{j}|a_{j}D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)}|)={\mathbb{E}}[|D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)}|^{3}].

By (A.78), we have

n24+e+μ12≤𝔼⁡[(D+μ1,j(0))2]≤n2+e+μ12;𝔼⁡[|D+μ1,j(0)|3]≤8​(ρ⁡(D+μ1,j(0))+|e+μ1|3)≤8​(n3/2+|e+μ1|3).\frac{n}{24}+e_{+\mu_{1}}^{2}\leq{\mathbb{E}}[(D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)})^{2}]\leq\frac{n}{2}+e_{+\mu_{1}}^{2};\quad{\mathbb{E}}[|D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)}|^{3}]\leq 8(\rho(D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)})+|e_{+\mu_{1}}|^{3})\leq 8(n^{3/2}+|e_{+\mu_{1}}|^{3}). (A.80)

Similarly, applying Berry-Esseen theorem, we have

ℙ⁡(|∑j=1maj​|aj​D+μ1,j(0)||>t)≤2​Φ¯​(t​mn+2​Cn​n​ε)+Cm,{\mathbb{P}}(\Big|\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_{j}|a_{j}D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)}|\Big|>t)\leq 2\bar{\Phi}\big(\frac{t\sqrt{m}}{\sqrt{n}+2C_{n}\sqrt{n\varepsilon}}\big)+\frac{C}{\sqrt{m}},

where the inequality uses Var​(m​aj​|aj​D+μ1,j(0)|)≤(n+|e+μ1|)2\text{Var}(ma_{j}|a_{j}D_{+\mu_{1},j}^{(0)}|)\leq(\sqrt{n}+|e_{+\mu_{1}}|)^{2} and (A.77). Then the results of this lemma are proved by noting that Cn​ε≥1C_{n}\sqrt{\varepsilon}\geq 1 for large enough nn. ∎

Theorem A.13.

Suppose that Assumptions (A1)-(A6) hold. With probability at least 1−O⁡(1/m)−O⁡(n−ε)1-O(1/\sqrt{m})-O(n^{-\varepsilon}) over the initialization of the weights and the generation of training data, after one iteration, the classifier sgn⁡(f⁡(x,W(1)))\operatorname{sgn}(f(x,W^{(1)})) exhibits a generalization risk with the following bounds:

12​(1−n−ε)≤ℙ(x,y)∼Pclean​(y≠sgn⁡(f⁡(x,W(1))))≤12​(1+n−ε).\tfrac{1}{2}(1-n^{-\varepsilon})\leq{\mathbb{P}}_{(x,y)\sim P_{\text{clean}}}(y\neq\operatorname{sgn}(f(x;W^{(1)})))\leq\tfrac{1}{2}(1+n^{-\varepsilon}).
Proof.

For any given training data X∈𝒢dataX\in\mathcal{G}_{\text{data}}, denote the expectation of Dν,j(0)D_{\nu,j}^{(0)} by eνe_{\nu}, i.e.

eν:=𝔼⁡[Dν,j(0)|X]=(cν−nν−c−ν+n−ν)/2,ν∈{±μ1,±μ2},e_{\nu}:={\mathbb{E}}[D_{\nu,j}^{(0)}|X]=(c_{\nu}-n_{\nu}-c_{-\nu}+n_{-\nu})/2,\quad\nu\in\{\pm\mu_{1},\pm\mu_{2}\}, (A.81)

and a set of parameters 𝒢X\mathcal{G}_{X}:

𝒢X:={(a,W(0)):|∑j=1maj​ϕ​(aj​Dν,j(0))−eν/2|≤3​Cn​n​ε/m​log⁡(m),|∑j=1maj|ajDν,j(0)||≤3Cnn​ε/mlog(m),a∈𝒢A,W(0)∈𝒢W}.\begin{split}\mathcal{G}_{X}:=\big\{(a,W^{(0)}):&|\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_{j}\phi(a_{j}D_{\nu,j}^{(0)})-e_{\nu}/2|\leq 3C_{n}\sqrt{n\varepsilon/m}\log(m),\\ &\big|\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_{j}|a_{j}D_{\nu,j}^{(0)}|\big|\leq 3C_{n}\sqrt{n\varepsilon/m}\log(m),a\in\mathcal{G}_{A},W^{(0)}\in\mathcal{G}_{W}\big\}.\end{split}

Applying the union bound, we have

ℙ⁡(𝒢X|X∈𝒢data)≥1−exp⁡(−Ω⁡(log2⁡(m)))−2​Cm−n−ε{\mathbb{P}}(\mathcal{G}_{X}|X\in\mathcal{G}_{\text{data}})\geq 1-\exp(-\Omega(\log^{2}(m)))-\frac{2C}{\sqrt{m}}-n^{-\varepsilon}

by Lemma A.12 and 4.3. Further we have

ℙ⁡((a,W(0))∈𝒢X,X∈𝒢data)≥ℙ⁡(𝒢X|X∈𝒢data)​ℙ​(X∈𝒢data)≥1−exp(−log2(m)/2)−2​Cm−2n−ε≥1−3​Cm−2​n−ε.\begin{split}{\mathbb{P}}((a,W^{(0)})\in\mathcal{G}_{X},X\in\mathcal{G}_{\text{data}})&\geq{\mathbb{P}}(\mathcal{G}_{X}|X\in\mathcal{G}_{\text{data}}){\mathbb{P}}(X\in\mathcal{G}_{\text{data}})\\ &\geq 1-\exp(-\log^{2}(m)/2)-\frac{2C}{\sqrt{m}}-2n^{-\varepsilon}\\ &\geq 1-\frac{3C}{\sqrt{m}}-2n^{-\varepsilon}.\end{split}

Define events ℱtest,ν\mathcal{F}_{{\text{test}},\nu} for test data:

ℱtest,ν={x∈ℝp:|‖x‖2−p−‖μ‖2|≤10​p​log⁡(n);|⟨x,xi⟩−⟨ν,x¯i⟩|≤10p​log⁡(n) for all i∈[n]},ν∈{±μ1,±μ2}.\begin{split}\mathcal{F}_{{\text{test}},\nu}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}^{p}:&|\|x\|^{2}-p-\|\mu\|^{2}|\leq 10\sqrt{p\log(n)};\\ &|\langle x,x_{i}\rangle-\langle\nu,\bar{x}_{i}\rangle|\leq 10\sqrt{p\log(n)}\text{ for all }i\in[n]\},\quad\nu\in\{\pm\mu_{1},\pm\mu_{2}\}.\end{split}

Treat {x}∪{xi}i=1n\{x\}\cup\{x_{i}\}_{i=1}^{n} as a new ‘training’ set with n+1n+1 datapoints. Following the proof procedure in Lemma 4.1, we can show that ℙx∼N⁡(ν,Ip)​(x∈ℱtest|X∈𝒢data)≥1−n−ε{\mathbb{P}}_{x\sim N(\nu,I_{p})}(x\in\mathcal{F}_{{\text{test}}}|X\in\mathcal{G}_{{\text{data}}})\geq 1-n^{-\varepsilon}, where ℱtest:=∪ν∈{±μ1,±μ2}ℱtest,ν\mathcal{F}_{{\text{test}}}:=\cup_{\nu\in\{\pm\mu_{1},\pm\mu_{2}\}}\mathcal{F}_{{\text{test}},\nu}. And ℱtest\mathcal{F}_{{\text{test}}} is a symmetric set for xx, i.e., if x∈ℱtestx\in\mathcal{F}_{{\text{test}}}, then −x-x also belongs to ℱtest\mathcal{F}_{{\text{test}}}. In the remaining proof, by convention all probabilities and expectations are implicitly conditioned on fixed X∈𝒢dataX\in\mathcal{G}_{\text{data}} and a,W(0)∈𝒢Xa,W^{(0)}\in\mathcal{G}_{X}. Therefore, to simplify notation, we write ℙ⁡(⋅){\mathbb{P}}(\,\cdot\,) and 𝔼⁡[⋅]{\mathbb{E}}[\,\cdot\,] to denote ℙ(⋅|a,W(0),{xi}){\mathbb{P}}(\,\cdot\,|a,W^{(0)},\{x_{i}\}) and 𝔼[⋅|a,W(0),{xi}]{\mathbb{E}}[\,\cdot\,|a,W^{(0)},\{x_{i}\}], respectively. In other words, the randomness is over the test data (x,y)(x,y), conditioned on a fixed initialization and training data. We first look at the clusters centered at ±μ1\pm\mu_{1}, i.e. x∼N⁡(±μ1,Ip),y=1x\sim N(\pm\mu_{1},I_{p}),y=1. Then we have

ℙx∼N⁡(±μ1,Ip)(y≠sgn(f(x,W(1))))=ℙx∼N⁡(±μ1,Ip)(f(x,W(1))≤0)=12​ℙx∼N⁡(μ1,Ip)​(f⁡(x,W(1))≤0)+12​ℙx∼N⁡(μ1,Ip)​(f⁡(−x,W(1))≤0).\begin{split}{\mathbb{P}}&{}_{x\sim N(\pm\mu_{1},I_{p})}(y\neq\operatorname{sgn}(f(x,W^{(1)})))={\mathbb{P}}_{x\sim N(\pm\mu_{1},I_{p})}(f(x,W^{(1)})\leq 0)\\ &=\frac{1}{2}{\mathbb{P}}_{x\sim N(\mu_{1},I_{p})}(f(x,W^{(1)})\leq 0)+\frac{1}{2}{\mathbb{P}}_{x\sim N(\mu_{1},I_{p})}(f(-x,W^{(1)})\leq 0).\end{split} (A.82)

Note that given W(0)W^{(0)} and XX, we have with probability 11 that

|f⁡(x,W(1))−f⁡(x,W(1)−W(0))|=|∑j=1maj​[ϕ⁡(⟨wj(1),x⟩)−ϕ⁡(⟨wj(1)−wj(0),x⟩)]|≤∑j=1m|aj​⟨wj(0),x⟩|≤∑j=1maj2​∑j=1m‖wj(0)‖2⋅‖x‖2=‖W(0)‖F⋅‖x‖≤ωinit​3​m​p/2​‖x‖,\begin{split}|f(x;W^{(1)})-f(x;W^{(1)}-W^{(0)})|&=\Big|\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_{j}[\phi(\langle w_{j}^{(1)},x\rangle)-\phi(\langle w_{j}^{(1)}-w_{j}^{(0)},x\rangle)]\Big|\\ &\leq\sum_{j=1}^{m}|a_{j}\langle w_{j}^{(0)},x\rangle|\leq\sqrt{\sum_{j=1}^{m}a_{j}^{2}\sum_{j=1}^{m}\|w_{j}^{(0)}\|^{2}\cdot\|x\|^{2}}\\ &=\|W^{(0)}\|_{F}\cdot\|x\|\leq\omega_{\text{init}}\sqrt{3mp/2}\|x\|,\end{split} (A.83)

where the first inequality comes from the 11-Lipschitz continuity of ϕ⁡(⋅)\phi(\cdot); the second inequality uses Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; and the last inequality uses Lemma 4.3. Next, recall that W𝚃W_{{\mathtt{T}}} is defined as in (A.72). By the same argument above, we have

A.6 Probability Lemmas

Lemma A.14.

Suppose we have a random variable gg that has finite L3L_{3} norm and a Rademacher variable aa that is independent with gg. Then we have

max⁡{12​Var​(g),14​(𝔼⁡[g])2}≤Var​(a​ϕ​(a​g))≤max⁡{Var​(g),12​(𝔼⁡[g])2};\max\{\frac{1}{2}\text{Var}(g),\frac{1}{4}({\mathbb{E}}[g])^{2}\}\leq\text{Var}(a\phi(ag))\leq\max\{\text{Var}(g),\frac{1}{2}({\mathbb{E}}[g])^{2}\}; (A.94)
𝔼[|aϕ(ag)−𝔼[aϕ(ag))]|3]≤32max{𝔼[|g−𝔼[g]|3],|𝔼[g]|3}.{\mathbb{E}}\big[\big|a\phi(ag)-{\mathbb{E}}[a\phi(ag))]\big|^{3}\big]\leq 32\max\{{\mathbb{E}}[|g-{\mathbb{E}}[g]|^{3}],|{\mathbb{E}}[g]|^{3}\}. (A.95)
Proof.

The expectation of the random variable a​ϕ​(a​g)a\phi(ag) is

𝔼⁡[a​ϕ​(a​g)]=12​𝔼​[ϕ⁡(g)−ϕ⁡(−g)]=12​𝔼​[g],{\mathbb{E}}[a\phi(ag)]=\frac{1}{2}{\mathbb{E}}[\phi(g)-\phi(-g)]=\frac{1}{2}{\mathbb{E}}[g], (A.96)

where the first equation uses the law of expectation, and the second equation uses ϕ⁡(x)−ϕ⁡(−x)=x.\phi(x)-\phi(-x)=x. The second moment of a​ϕ​(a​g)a\phi(ag) is

𝔼⁡[(a​ϕ​(a​g))2]=𝔼⁡[ϕ​(a​g)2]=12​𝔼​[ϕ​(g)2+ϕ​(−g)2]=12​𝔼​[g2],{\mathbb{E}}[(a\phi(ag))^{2}]={\mathbb{E}}[\phi(ag)^{2}]=\frac{1}{2}{\mathbb{E}}[\phi(g)^{2}+\phi(-g)^{2}]=\frac{1}{2}{\mathbb{E}}[g^{2}], (A.97)

where the last equation uses ϕ​(x)2+ϕ​(−x)2=x2.\phi(x)^{2}+\phi(-x)^{2}=x^{2}. Combining (A.96) and (A.97), we have

Var​(a​ϕ​(a​g))=12​𝔼​[g2]−14​(𝔼⁡[g])2=12​Var​(g)+14​(𝔼⁡[g])2,\text{Var}(a\phi(ag))=\frac{1}{2}{\mathbb{E}}[g^{2}]-\frac{1}{4}({\mathbb{E}}[g])^{2}=\frac{1}{2}\text{Var}(g)+\frac{1}{4}({\mathbb{E}}[g])^{2},

which implies (A.94). Moreover, for a random variable XX that has finite L3L_{3} norm, we have

‖X−𝔼⁡[X]‖3≤‖X‖3+‖𝔼⁡[X]‖3≤‖X‖3+𝔼⁡[|X|]≤2​‖X‖3,\|X-{\mathbb{E}}[X]\|_{3}\leq\|X\|_{3}+\|{\mathbb{E}}[X]\|_{3}\leq\|X\|_{3}+{\mathbb{E}}[|X|]\leq 2\|X\|_{3},

where the second inequality is due to ‖𝔼⁡[X]‖3=|𝔼⁡[X]|\|{\mathbb{E}}[X]\|_{3}=|{\mathbb{E}}[X]| and the last inequality is due to ‖X‖1≤‖X‖3\|X\|_{1}\leq\|X\|_{3}. Thus we have

𝔼⁡[|a​ϕ​(a​g)−12​𝔼​[g]|3]≤8​𝔼​[|a​ϕ​(a​g)|3]=4​𝔼​[ϕ​(g)3+ϕ​(−g)3]=4​𝔼​[|g|3],{\mathbb{E}}\big[\big|a\phi(ag)-\frac{1}{2}{\mathbb{E}}[g]\big|^{3}\big]\leq 8{\mathbb{E}}[|a\phi(ag)|^{3}]=4{\mathbb{E}}[\phi(g)^{3}+\phi(-g)^{3}]=4{\mathbb{E}}[|g|^{3}],

where the last equation is due to ϕ​(x)3+ϕ​(−x)3=|x|3.\phi(x)^{3}+\phi(-x)^{3}=|x|^{3}. Then by ‖g‖3≤‖g−𝔼⁡[g]‖3+|𝔼⁡[g]|\|g\|_{3}\leq\|g-{\mathbb{E}}[g]\|_{3}+|{\mathbb{E}}[g]|, we have

𝔼⁡[|a​ϕ​(a​g)−12​𝔼​[g]|3]≤4​(‖g−𝔼⁡[g]‖3+|𝔼⁡[g]|)3≤32​max​{𝔼⁡[|g−𝔼⁡[g]|3],|𝔼⁡[g]|3}.{\mathbb{E}}\big[\big|a\phi(ag)-\frac{1}{2}{\mathbb{E}}[g]\big|^{3}\big]\leq 4\big(\|g-{\mathbb{E}}[g]\|_{3}+|{\mathbb{E}}[g]|\big)^{3}\leq 32\max\{{\mathbb{E}}[|g-{\mathbb{E}}[g]|^{3}],|{\mathbb{E}}[g]|^{3}\}.

Lemma A.15.

Suppose Z=[z1,⋯,zn]⊤∼N⁡(0,Σ)Z=[z_{1},\cdots,z_{n}]^{\top}\sim N(0,\Sigma), where Σi​i=1, and ​|Σi​j|≤1/(C​n2),1≤i≠j≤n.\Sigma_{ii}=1,\text{ and }|\Sigma_{ij}|\leq 1/(Cn^{2}),1\leq i\neq j\leq n. And Z′=[z1′,⋯,zn′]⊤∼N⁡(0,𝕀n)Z^{\prime}=[z_{1}^{\prime},\cdots,z_{n}^{\prime}]^{\top}\sim N(0,\mathbb{I}_{n}). Let bi=𝕀⁡(zi>0)​ and ​bi′=𝕀⁡(zi′>0),i∈[n]b_{i}=\mathbb{I}(z_{i}>0)\text{ and }b_{i}^{\prime}=\mathbb{I}(z_{i}^{\prime}>0),i\in[n] be Bernoulli random variables. Let B=[b1,⋯,bn]⊤B=[b_{1},\cdots,b_{n}]^{\top} and B′=[b1′,⋯,bn′]⊤B^{\prime}=[b_{1}^{\prime},\cdots,b_{n}^{\prime}]^{\top}. Then we have that for any non-negative function f:ℝn→ℝ+∪{0}f:\mathbb{R}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{+}\cup\{0\},

12​𝔼B′​[f⁡(b1′,⋯,bn′)]≤𝔼B​[f⁡(b1,⋯,bn)]≤2​𝔼B′​[f⁡(b1′,⋯,bn′)].\frac{1}{2}{\mathbb{E}}_{B^{\prime}}[f(b_{1}^{\prime},\cdots,b_{n}^{\prime})]\leq{\mathbb{E}}_{B}[f(b_{1},\cdots,b_{n})]\leq 2{\mathbb{E}}_{B^{\prime}}[f(b_{1}^{\prime},\cdots,b_{n}^{\prime})].
Proof.

Note that for any fixed value (b1,⋯,bn)∈{0,1}n(b_{1},\cdots,b_{n})\in\{0,1\}^{n}, ℙB′​(b1′,⋯,bn′)=(1/2)n{\mathbb{P}}_{B^{\prime}}(b_{1}^{\prime},\cdots,b_{n}^{\prime})=(1/2)^{n}. Then we have

𝔼B​[f⁡(b1,⋯,bn)]=∑b1,⋯,bnf⁡(b1,⋯,bn)​ℙB​(b1,⋯,bn)≥(2​γ1)n​∑b1,⋯,bnf⁡(b1,⋯,bn)​ℙB′​(b1,⋯,bn)=(2​γ1)n​𝔼B′​[f⁡(b1,⋯,bn)],\begin{split}{\mathbb{E}}_{B}[f(b_{1},\cdots,b_{n})]&=\sum_{b_{1},\cdots,b_{n}}f(b_{1},\cdots,b_{n}){\mathbb{P}}_{B}(b_{1},\cdots,b_{n})\\ &\geq(2\gamma_{1})^{n}\sum_{b_{1},\cdots,b_{n}}f(b_{1},\cdots,b_{n}){\mathbb{P}}_{B^{\prime}}(b_{1},\cdots,b_{n})\\ &=(2\gamma_{1})^{n}{\mathbb{E}}_{B^{\prime}}[f(b_{1},\cdots,b_{n})],\end{split} (A.98)

where the inequality comes from Lemma A.16. On the other side, similarly we have

𝔼B​[f⁡(b1,⋯,bn)]≤(2​γ2)n​𝔼B′​[f⁡(b1,⋯,bn)].{\mathbb{E}}_{B}[f(b_{1},\cdots,b_{n})]\leq(2\gamma_{2})^{n}{\mathbb{E}}_{B^{\prime}}[f(b_{1},\cdots,b_{n})]. (A.99)

By C>8C>8, we have (2​γ1)n=(1−4/(C​n))n≥1−4/(C​n)≥1/2(2\gamma_{1})^{n}=(1-4/(Cn))^{n}\geq 1-4/(Cn)\geq 1/2 and (2​γ2)n=(1+4/(C​n))n≤exp⁡(4/C)≤exp⁡(1/2)≤2(2\gamma_{2})^{n}=(1+4/(Cn))^{n}\leq\exp(4/C)\leq\exp(1/2)\leq 2. Combining these results with (A.98) and (A.99), we have

12​𝔼B′​[f⁡(b1′,⋯,bn′)]≤𝔼B​[f⁡(b1,⋯,bn)]≤2​𝔼B′​[f⁡(b1′,⋯,bn′)].\frac{1}{2}{\mathbb{E}}_{B^{\prime}}[f(b_{1}^{\prime},\cdots,b_{n}^{\prime})]\leq{\mathbb{E}}_{B}[f(b_{1},\cdots,b_{n})]\leq 2{\mathbb{E}}_{B^{\prime}}[f(b_{1}^{\prime},\cdots,b_{n}^{\prime})].

Lemma A.16.

Suppose Z=[z1,⋯,zn]⊤∼N⁡(0,Σ)Z=[z_{1},\cdots,z_{n}]^{\top}\sim N(0,\Sigma), where Σi​i=1, and ​|Σi​j|≤1/(C​n2),1≤i≠j≤n.\Sigma_{ii}=1,\text{ and }|\Sigma_{ij}|\leq 1/(Cn^{2}),1\leq i\neq j\leq n. Then we have that for any subset 𝒜⊆[n]{\mathcal{A}}\subseteq[n],

γ1n≤𝔼⁡[∏i∈𝒜𝕀⁡(zi>0)⋅∏i∈[n]\𝒜𝕀⁡(zi<0)]≤γ2n\gamma_{1}^{n}\leq{\mathbb{E}}[\prod_{i\in{\mathcal{A}}}\mathbb{I}(z_{i}>0)\cdot\prod_{i\in[n]\backslash{\mathcal{A}}}\mathbb{I}(z_{i}<0)]\leq\gamma_{2}^{n}

for γ1=1/2−2/(C​n)\gamma_{1}=1/2-2/(Cn) and γ2=1/2+2/(C​n)\gamma_{2}=1/2+2/(Cn).

Proof.

We first prove the result for 𝒜=[n]{\mathcal{A}}=[n]. Note that

ℙ⁡(z1>0,⋯,zn>0)=ℙ⁡(z1>0)​∏k=2nℙ⁡(zk>0|zk−1>0,⋯,z1>0).{\mathbb{P}}(z_{1}>0,\cdots,z_{n}>0)={\mathbb{P}}(z_{1}>0)\prod_{k=2}^{n}{\mathbb{P}}(z_{k}>0|z_{k-1}>0,\cdots,z_{1}>0). (A.100)

Let Zk−1=[z1,⋯,zk−1]⊤Z_{k-1}=[z_{1},\cdots,z_{k-1}]^{\top} and denote the covariance matrix of [z1,⋯,zk][z_{1},\cdots,z_{k}] as

[Σk−1ϵkϵk⊤1],\begin{split}\left[\begin{array}[]{cc}\Sigma_{k-1}&\epsilon_{k}\\ \epsilon_{k}^{\top}&1\end{array}\right],\end{split}

where Σk−1=Cov​(Zk−1)\Sigma_{k-1}=\text{Cov}(Z_{k-1}) and ϵk=Cov​(Zk−1,zk)\epsilon_{k}=\text{Cov}(Z_{k-1},z_{k}). Then |ϵk​j|≤1/(C​n2)|\epsilon_{kj}|\leq 1/(Cn^{2}) for j∈[k−1]j\in[k-1], and the conditional distribution of zk|Zk−1z_{k}|Z_{k-1} is N⁡(ϵk⊤​Σk−1−1​Zk−1,1−ϵk⊤​Σk−1−1​ϵk)N(\epsilon_{k}^{\top}\Sigma_{k-1}^{-1}Z_{k-1},1-\epsilon_{k}^{\top}\Sigma_{k-1}^{-1}\epsilon_{k}). By Gershgorin circle theorem, we have

1−1C​n≤λmin​(Σk−1)≤λmax​(Σk−1)≤1+1C​n.1-\frac{1}{Cn}\leq\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{k-1})\leq\lambda_{\max}(\Sigma_{k-1})\leq 1+\frac{1}{Cn}.

Denote fk−1​(⋅)f_{k-1}(\cdot) as the density function of Zk−1Z_{k-1}. Then we have

for sufficiently large nn. Here the second inequality uses |Φ⁡(x)−Φ⁡(0)|≤Φ′​(0)​|x||\Phi(x)-\Phi(0)|\leq\Phi^{\prime}(0)|x| and Cauchy-Schwarz inequality; the third inequality uses σmin​(Σk−1)=λmin​(Σk−1)≥1/2\sigma_{\min}(\Sigma_{k-1})=\lambda_{\min}(\Sigma_{k-1})\geq 1/2 and ∥Σk−1−1/2ϵk∥≤2∥ϵk∥≤2n−3/2/C\|\Sigma_{k-1}^{-1/2}\epsilon_{k}\|\leq\sqrt{2}\|\epsilon_{k}\|\leq\sqrt{2}n^{-3/2}/C; and the fourth inequality uses the concentration inequality for chi-square random variables in Lemma A.17. Then the result is proved by combining (A.100) and (A.101). On the other side, we have

Note that our proof does not use any information related to 𝒜{\mathcal{A}}, thus we can extend the result for any subset 𝒜⊆[n]{\mathcal{A}}\subseteq[n]. ∎

Lemma A.17.

For Xk​ i.i.d∼N⁡(0,σ2),1≤k≤nX_{k}\text{ i.i.d}\sim N(0,\sigma^{2}),1\leq k\leq n, we have

Φ′(t)/t≤ℙ(|X1|≥tσ)≤exp(−t2/2),∀t≥1;\Phi^{\prime}(t)/t\leq{\mathbb{P}}(|X_{1}|\geq t\sigma)\leq\exp(-t^{2}/2),\quad\forall t\geq 1;
ℙ(|1n​σ2∑k=1nXk2−1|≥t)≤2exp(−nt2/8),∀t∈(0,1).{\mathbb{P}}(\big|\frac{1}{n\sigma^{2}}\sum_{k=1}^{n}X_{k}^{2}-1\big|\geq t)\leq 2\exp(-nt^{2}/8),\quad\forall t\in(0,1).
Proof.

For the first inequality, we note that

Φ¯​(t)=∫t+∞x2​π​x​exp⁡(−12​x2)​𝑑x≤∫t+∞12​2​π​t​exp⁡(−12​x2)​d​x2=Φ′​(t)t.\bar{\Phi}(t)=\int_{t}^{+\infty}\frac{x}{\sqrt{2\pi}x}\exp(-\frac{1}{2}x^{2})dx\leq\int_{t}^{+\infty}\frac{1}{2\sqrt{2\pi}t}\exp(-\frac{1}{2}x^{2})dx^{2}=\frac{\Phi^{\prime}(t)}{t}.

It yields that for any t≥1t\geq 1,

ℙ(|X1|≥tσ)=2Φ¯(t)≤2Φ′(t)/t≤exp(−t2/2).{\mathbb{P}}(|X_{1}|\geq t\sigma)=2\bar{\Phi}(t)\leq 2\Phi^{\prime}(t)/t\leq\exp(-t^{2}/2).

On the other side, we have

Φ¯​(t)≥∫t+∞1+x2x22​π​1+t2t2​exp⁡(−12​x2)​𝑑x=12​π​t21+t2​(−exp⁡(−x22)x)|x=t+∞=t1+t2​Φ′​(t).\bar{\Phi}(t)\geq\int_{t}^{+\infty}\frac{\frac{1+x^{2}}{x^{2}}}{\sqrt{2\pi}\frac{1+t^{2}}{t^{2}}}\exp(-\frac{1}{2}x^{2})dx=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\frac{t^{2}}{1+t^{2}}\Big(-\frac{\exp(-\frac{x^{2}}{2})}{x}\Big)\Big|_{x=t}^{+\infty}=\frac{t}{1+t^{2}}\Phi^{\prime}(t).

When t≥1t\geq 1, it further yields that Φ¯​(t)≥Φ′​(t)/(2​t)\bar{\Phi}(t)\geq\Phi^{\prime}(t)/(2t). Thus we have

ℙ⁡(|X1|≥t​σ)=2​Φ¯​(t)≥Φ′​(t)/t.{\mathbb{P}}(|X_{1}|\geq t\sigma)=2\bar{\Phi}(t)\geq\Phi^{\prime}(t)/t.

The second inequality is Example 2.11 in [Wai19] ∎

Lemma A.18 (Hoeffding’s inequality, Equation (2.11) in [Wai19]).

Let Xk,1≤k≤nX_{k},1\leq k\leq n be a series of independent random variables with Xk∈[a,b]X_{k}\in[a,b]. Then

ℙ⁡(∑k=1n(Xk−𝔼⁡[Xk])≥t)≤exp⁡(−2​t2n​(b−a)2),∀t≥0.{\mathbb{P}}(\sum_{k=1}^{n}(X_{k}-{\mathbb{E}}[X_{k}])\geq t)\leq\exp\Big(-\frac{2t^{2}}{n(b-a)^{2}}\Big),\quad\forall t\geq 0.
Lemma A.19.

[Berry-Esseen Theorem, Theorem 3.4.17 in [Dur19]] Let X1,⋯,XnX_{1},\cdots,X_{n} are i.i.d. random variables with 𝔼⁡[Xi]=0,Var​(Xi)=σ2{\mathbb{E}}[X_{i}]=0,\text{Var}(X_{i})=\sigma^{2}, and 𝔼⁡[|Xi|3]=ρ<∞{\mathbb{E}}[|X_{i}|^{3}]=\rho<\infty. If Fn​(x)F_{n}(x) is the distribution of ∑i=1nXi/(σ​n)\sum_{i=1}^{n}X_{i}/(\sigma\sqrt{n}), then

|Fn​(x)−Φ⁡(x)|≤3​ρσ3​n.|F_{n}(x)-\Phi(x)|\leq\frac{3\rho}{\sigma^{3}\sqrt{n}}.
